bio.en: Andrew “Boz” Bosworth is CTO of Meta, one of its first engineers (2006), and creator of landmark products including the Facebook News Feed, mobile ads platform, and Messenger.
bio.zh: Andrew “Boz” Bosworth 是 Meta 首席技术官，公司最早的工程师之一（2006 年加入），并打造了 Facebook 动态消息、移动广告平台和 Messenger 等标志性产品。

summary.en: Boz reflects on the brutal early days of Facebook—120-hour weeks, no hobbies—and why the romantic founder story hides the grind. He shares lessons on asking your manager for help, why communication is the job, and stories from building the very first News Feed (which users hated yet immediately doubled usage). The conversation also covers Meta's recent turnaround, his thoughts on Apple Vision Pro, and broad leadership and career advice.
summary.zh: Boz 回顾了 Facebook 早期残酷的日子——每周 120 小时、没有爱好——以及为何浪漫的创始人故事掩盖了其中的煎熬。他分享了向经理求助、为何“沟通就是工作”的经验，以及打造第一个动态消息（用户讨厌却立即令使用量翻倍）的故事。对话还涵盖 Meta 近期的扭亏为盈、对 Apple Vision Pro 的看法，以及广泛的领导与职业建议。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: I didn't sleep for more than four hours at a time. I'd wake up every four hours and check the report and see if anyone was attacking the site. They don't tell you about that stuff in the movies.

turns.zh: 你每周工作120个小时，一点个人爱好都没有。

turns.en: I don't want to take away from the romanticism of it. It's just that most often, we hear those romantic stories from the successes. It's a healthy thing for people to want to throw themselves into something and take that risk, but it is not glamorous at the time.
turns.zh: 我无意贬低其中的浪漫色彩。只是我们往往只听闻成功者的光彩故事。人们愿意全身心投入、甘冒风险固然值得称赞，但当下这份激情可不那么光鲜亮丽。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The newsfeed. That was one of your early projects at Facebook. People did not want it. They were wrong, clearly.
turns.zh: 新闻推送功能是你在Facebook早期参与的项目之一。当时用户并不买账，但显然他们错了。

turns.en: Now, newsfeed was an easier case than people suspect. Everyone was outraged at the same time as they immediately doubled their usage of the product.
turns.zh: 其实新闻推送功能的成功比人们想象得要容易得多。用户对新功能的狂热反响，让产品的使用量瞬间翻倍。

turns.zh: 可能就是这个了。你大学时是全国跆拳道冠军。大学里你还给马克·扎克伯格当过助教，教授AI课程，但据我所知，这并不是你进入Facebook的真正原因。哈佛大学当时招你去踢足球。高中时你积极参与4-H俱乐部，养过动物，还在县集市上展示过成果。你还曾和大卫·科波菲尔同台表演。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: That's true.
turns.zh: 是真的。

turns.zh: MC Hammer曾称赞你的穿搭很时尚。乔治·W·布什总统还夸过你的鞋子和头发有光泽。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth

turns.zh: 是的，这些都是真的。我想说，哇。首先，我得确保大家明白，我是大学国家冠军，当时是绿腰带级别，这就像是初级冠军。这样大家就能清楚这是什么意思了。

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Heavyweight sparring. I'll tell... The prom story is a funny one. It's related to the 4-H story. I was a big-time 4-H'er, National 4-H Hall of Fame, did all this stuff there. (00:06:29): As a comeup to that, 4-H is a wonderful program, youth program, it's coed program, and I was all over the state, all over the country, doing leadership events and doing these conferences, and doing a lot of public speaking. (00:06:39): And almost every 4-H event has a dance. People don't know that. At the end of a conference, at the end of the, literally camp, you'd go camping for a week, at the end there's a dance. (00:06:49): And so, as a consequence, the most important thing, if wanted to go to a lot of proms, I was a good dancer. And it turns out, the high-level bit, at least in the 1990s, for girls selecting who they might want to go to prom with was, will he and can he dance? And the answer with me was yes. And combine that with the fact that I knew a bunch of girls who went to different schools, that's the recipe for success right there, if that's the goal that somebody has. Two my junior year and 12 my senior year. I once went to three in one weekend, a Friday, a Saturday, and a Sunday night.
turns.zh: 重量级对抗赛。我来讲讲……那个毕业舞会的故事很有趣。这和4-H的故事有关。我曾是4-H的忠实成员，还入选了4-H名人堂，在那里做过很多事。（00:06:29）顺便说一句，4-H是一个很棒的项目，是面向青少年的综合性项目，我在全州、全国各地参加领导力活动和会议，做过很多公开演讲。（00:06:39）几乎每个4-H活动都有舞会。大家可能不知道，在会议结束时，在露营结束时——我们要露营一周，结束时总会有舞会。（00:06:49）所以，关键是，如果我想去很多毕业舞会，我就得是个不错的舞者。结果发现，至少在90年代，女孩们选择舞伴时最看重的是对方是否会跳舞、跳得好不好。我的答案是会。再加上我认识很多不同学校的女孩，这就是成功秘诀，如果这是某人的目标的话。大三时去了两次，毕业那年去了12次。我有一次一个周末去了三个舞会——周五、周六、周日晚上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Another fun fact about you is you were basically the 10th engineer at Facebook, initially, way before it was a clear success story. I imagine there was a lot of pain and suffering and struggle that people don't often hear about those early days. They see a movie like The Social Network. It looks like, "Oh, that was so much fun. I've got to start a company. It's going to become a trillion-dollar success story." I'm curious just what those early days were like. Are there memories that stand out to you?
turns.zh: 关于你的另一个趣事是，你最初是Facebook的第十位工程师，那时公司还远未成为如今的成功典范。我想早期那些岁月充满了痛苦、煎熬和挣扎，而人们却不常听闻这些故事。他们看《社交网络》这样的电影时，会觉得"哦，那真是太有趣了。我也要去创办公司，成就千亿美元的传奇。"我很好奇那些早期岁月究竟是怎样的。有没有什么难忘的回忆？

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Yeah, there's a bit of a joke in the 10th thing, which is me and five other guys all joined at the same time, and there was nine engineers before us. We joined the same day, so we're all the 10th engineer. So, somewhere between 10 and 16, depending on how you want to do the numeration on that. (00:07:59): I've written about this in my blog, and I tell this story a lot, which is it was fun, and there was tremendous camaraderie and memories that were formed, but they were formed in a kind of forge of really intense times. (00:08:13): At that time, almost all of us lived within one mile of the office. We ate most of our meals together because we were working, not to say we weren't also friends, but because we were working, it's like, oh cool, you just roll into a meal and roll back into work. (00:08:26): And there's little things that you don't appreciate, which is like there was nobody to help you. There was no expert. And so, it wasn't like, "Hey, I'm struggling with this one tricky problem. Who should I talk to?" It's like, nobody. You should talk to yourself and figure this out. Or it's like, "Oh, man. My servers are out of capacity." It's like, "Cool. You should go to Fry's Electronics, you should buy a bunch of components, you should build a new server, and then you should run it. Maybe drive into the colo, rack it, and then get back and run it." (00:08:52): People really undervalue the fact that when you go to work, even a moderate mid-size corporation today, especially with the tremendous growth of startups supporting startups, things like payroll and finance and IT and HR, these things are professionally handled in many cases. (00:09:10): That was just not the case in the early 2000s. It was just you, and your personal car, and whatever you wanted to do with your time. (00:09:18): So, I don't want to take away from the romanticism of it, it's just that it's most often we hear those romantic stories from the successes. We so rarely hear somebody who went through really sacrificing a lot of my 20s from any kind of social or outgoing, fun environment. (00:09:37): It paid off for me, so no one feels bad for me, nor should they. But there are other people who do the exact same thing, maybe they worked harder, maybe they were smarter, maybe they did better, and it didn't play out for them. And it's a big sacrifice. (00:09:48): And so, I love the enthusiasm for startups, I love startup culture. I think it's a healthy thing for people to want to throw themselves into something and take that risk. But it is not glamorous at the time. In retrospect, it's like, "Oh, it can be..." We have a little halo around it. But at the time, it doesn't feel glamorous.
turns.zh: 是的，关于第十位工程师这个梗有点意思，当时我和另外五个人同时加入，而在我们之前已经有九位工程师了。我们同一天入职，所以都算第十位工程师。具体数字可能在10到16之间，取决于你怎么计算。（00:07:59）：我在博客里写过这段经历，也经常讲起。当时确实很有趣，同事间情谊深厚，留下了许多回忆，但这些回忆是在高强度奋斗的熔炉中铸就的。（00:08:13）：那时几乎所有人都住在离办公室一英里范围内。我们大部分餐都一起吃，因为要工作——不是说我们不交际，而是工作占据了生活，早上一起吃早餐，晚上继续工作，很方便。（00:08:26）：有些小细节被忽视了，比如没人能帮忙解决问题。没有专家指导。遇到难题时不会有人说：“嘿，我卡在这儿了，该找谁帮忙？”只能自己钻研。服务器超负荷时，只能自己去Fry's Electronics买零件组装新服务器，再运到机房安装。（00:08:52）：现在即使是中型公司，专业团队也处理好薪资、财务、IT、人力等事务，但21世纪初并非如此。当时全靠自己，靠私家车出行，靠利用业余时间。（00:09:18）：我不想贬低那些成功故事的浪漫色彩，但人们往往只听成功者的传奇，却鲜闻那些为事业牺牲了20岁青春、远离社交与娱乐环境的人的奋斗史。（00:09:37）：对我而言一切都是值得的，我不期望他人同情，但确实有人做着同样的事，或许更努力、更聪明、表现更出色，却未能成功。这是巨大的牺牲。（00:09:48）：所以我热爱创业的激情，喜欢创业文化。我认为人们愿意投身其中、承担风险是件健康的事，但当时确实不光彩。回首往事，我们会说"哦，这其实挺……"但当时真不觉得有魅力。

I had to wake up every four hours and check the report, and to see if anyone was attacking the site. And if they were, I was up, and I had to go battle back. And if they weren't, cool, I'd go back to sleep. But that's the thing, they don't tell you about that stuff in the movies.
turns.zh: 是啊。我们为了弥补损失喝了不少酒，所以我胖了不少……而你当时饮食也不健康。简直太疯狂了。（00:10:22）我觉得我之前讲过这个故事。有一段时间，我最先开发的项目之一就是反垃圾邮件、反爬虫的防护机制。但当时我们没有运维支持，也没有全天候的在线客服。（00:10:35）所以我开发了这个工具。当时我每隔四小时就得醒一次。整整两年，我每天睡眠时间从未超过四个小时。每隔四小时我就得醒来看报告，查看是否有攻击者在攻击网站。如果有攻击，我就得立刻反击；如果没有，那就继续睡。但关键是，电影里可不会告诉你这些现实情况。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's almost worse than having a kid, a newborn.
turns.zh: 这比养个新生儿还要糟糕。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: And nobody asked me to do it. Nobody even asked me to do the anti-spam, anti-scraping stuff. I just thought it was a problem, and I went and did that, and that was the solution I come with. If I was a better engineer, maybe I'd have solved a better problem.
turns.zh: 而且没人让我做这些事。甚至没人让我负责反垃圾邮件、反爬虫的工作。只是我觉得这是个问题，就主动去解决了。如果我是个更出色的工程师，或许能解决更复杂的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, maybe just to close out that thread, when you talk to founders, what advice do you give them along these lines?
turns.zh: 那么，关于这个话题，最后再问一句：当你和创始人交流时，你会给他们哪些方面的建议？

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: I want to be cautious about this, because what I tell founders... The first thing I tell founders is that I've never been a founder, and I want to recognize the difference. I joined January 9th, 2006. That's almost two years after Mark started the company. I wasn't involved with fundraising, I didn't have to do any of that side of the things, and I didn't even have to deal with the board or the business side of things. I really was lucky, in a way, to have joined when I did. (00:11:42): But the first thing I tell founders is like, "You should take my advice with a grain of salt. I have not actually been in your shoes." (00:11:47): If I can compliment you, really, one of the things I like about your program is, there's a whole system of professionals in our industry. And when I grew up in technology in the valley, you always heard about the ACM, right? The Association of Computing Machinery. You heard of these legendary professional organizations that supported people in our fields. (00:12:09): And by the nature of the rapid pace of change in the technology, and the nature of the engagement of those institutions, even academics, even academia broadly, kind of are out of touch. The tools that you got from those places weren't useful in our field. (00:12:23): So, I do think the mentorship that we give each other has been a critical and sustaining resource. There is, today, now, resources like your podcasts and your newsletter that are actually really designed to help people who are professionals in our industry in a way that is almost kind of missing for 15, 20 years, and I love to see that. Because if you're an up-and-coming [inaudible 00:12:45], literally you used to have to know somebody and ask them a question. (00:12:48): And so, a lot of times what I'm helping founders with, I can help them with the strategy, I can help them think through the technology choices, I can help through business, I can think through the management, the organization structure. But I also try to be very clear, there's a bunch of stuff that I just was never exposed to. (00:13:00): So, even as we just talk about how tough it was for the average engineer joining Facebook in 2006, man, it was even tougher for Mark Zuckerberg in 2004, probably. And that's a story that's been told, I'm sure, but still. So, I think these are both... It's almost all scale and variant. No matter how far you dial back, the challenges are interesting and are worth talking about.
turns.zh: 关于这件事，我得谨慎些，因为我给创始人提的建议……我首先要告诉创始人，我自己从未当过创始人，我得承认这两者的区别。我2006年1月9日加入公司，那时距离马克创办公司已经过去了将近两年。我当时不参与融资事宜，不需要处理那些附带工作，也无需应对董事会或商业层面的决策。某种程度上，我很幸运能在那个时机加入公司。（00:11:42）但我对创始人说的第一句话是：“你最好对我的建议持保留态度。我毕竟没亲身经历过你们的处境。” （00:11:47）如果要称赞你们的话，我很欣赏你们的项目，因为我们行业内有完善的专业体系。在硅谷科技圈成长的过程中，你总能听说ACM（美国计算机协会）之类的传奇组织。这些专业机构为业内人士提供了支持，但由于科技变革的快速性和相关机构（包括学术界）的滞后性，从这些机构获取的工具在我们的领域往往派不上用场。（00:12:09）所以，我认为我们彼此间的导师互助是至关重要且持续有效的资源。如今，像你们的播客和新闻通讯这样的资源，正是为业内专业人士量身打造的，这种支持体系在15-20年前几乎不存在，我很欣喜看到这样的改变。因为如果你是新晋的[音频中断00:12:45]，过去你往往需要认识业内人士才能获取帮助。（00:12:48）所以，我能为创始人提供战略指导，帮助他们评估技术选型，处理商业问题和管理架构，但我也会坦率地承认，有些领域我从未接触过。（00:13:00）即便我们谈论2006年加入Facebook的普通工程师所面临的挑战，马克·扎克伯格在2004年遇到的困难恐怕更大。虽然这段故事已被多次讲述，但仍值得回味。因此，我认为这两者……本质上都是规模和变体的问题。无论你回溯到何时，挑战都值得探讨和反思。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One of maybe your most popular posts is this quote that you share about the advice you often give. What you say is, "The advice I find I have to give more frequently than any other in my career, as a manager, a board member, an advisor and a friend, is for people to more directly leverage their leaders." Can you talk about that and what that means, and what that looks like?
turns.zh: 或许你最受欢迎的帖子之一，就是你分享的这段建议语录。你曾说过：“在我的职业生涯中，无论是作为管理者、董事会成员、顾问还是朋友，我发现自己最常给出的建议，就是让人们更直接地发挥其领导者的潜力。” 能否请你详细解读一下这句话的含义，以及具体的实践方式？

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: It's such a normal and natural healthy thing. And by the way, we do it in our personal relationships. Like I said in the post, we want to do it ourselves. We want to do it ourselves to prove to everyone that we can do it ourselves. (00:13:52): And we think in our heads, "If I ask for help, haven't I already given up that goal? Haven't I just admitted defeat on one of my top level goals, which is to demonstrate that I can do it myself?" (00:14:04): But what so often we forget is, more often than not, your job is not to do it yourself. Your job is to get it done, is to have the thing done, done well, done right, done competently. And a lot of times, the tools that you need to do that live with your manager, with your partner, with your advisor, with your mentor. That's where they live. (00:14:25): So, how many times as a manager have I gone through, and somebody's told them, "Here's the job." They're like, "I got it." They go off, they come back, it's done, it's wrong. And I'm not blaming them for it being wrong. They didn't check in with me. They misunderstood. We miscommunicated. I'll take the L on that. That's no problem. (00:14:42): But here we are, six months later, it's not done right because they misunderstood the brief. We miscommunicated with the brief. (00:14:49): Or they come back, and it took a year. And I'm like, "Why did this take a year instead of six months?" And they're like, "Oh, man. I had all these things I had to deal with." Where, if they had emailed me, I could have bulldozed that stuff. I could have cleared the path. I could have said, " Oh, no, no, no. Don't worry about that. This is the thing." And then we'd have been done six months sooner, and they would've been less frustrated. And so, light touches. (00:15:09): Now, I do think as a manager we also have a job to say, "Hey, that's kind of the work, so you got to kind of go figure that out." And one of my things I always tell my managers, one of the most powerful things we do is refuse to rule. Someone will bring me a thing. A lot of times we feel obligated to weigh in and help. I'll be like, "Nope, but look, I think you've got it. I think the challenges you're facing are the right challenges. I think you're approaching it in the right way. Just do your best there." And that's what it is. And so, there is a responsibility as well for those of us who are leaders, mentors, advisors, board members to do that. (00:15:39): But, by the way, we do this... Personal relationships. You're with your partner, and you're trying to do something the right way, but you're not talking to them about it. You're just taking a huge risk there, and for very little reward. They're not going to be mad if you ask them, like, "Hey, is this how you wanted it done? I don't know." (00:15:56): And so, I do think it's kind of funny how much we build these castles in our mind, these little silos that keep us from engaging the structures that are built around us, that are designed to help us succeed. I saw this great quote, actually just yesterday. I saw Patrick Stewart, who is one of my favorite actors of all time, and whose characters I love, and he talked about people going on casting calls. And this is a brutal thing for actors, right? You're going on 30, 40 things, you're getting rejected. It's tough. Everyone's kind of heard about this. And he said, "No one wants you to succeed more than the person you are auditioning for, because they want you to be awesome. Because as soon as you are awesome, they're done. They want you to be amazing." (00:16:37): That's like your manager. Nobody wants you to be more awesome than your manager does, because when you're amazing, your manager, his life gets easier, her life gets easier. So, I just think that's the mentality we get into is like, "No, no, no. They're testing me." They're not. They are rooting for you. I promise you that.
turns.zh:
这是一件再正常不过、再自然不过的健康之事。我这么说吧，我们在个人关系中也会这样做。正如我在帖子中所说，我们想自己动手，就是要向所有人证明我们能独自完成任务。（00:13:52）：但我们常忽视的一点是，多数时候你的职责并非亲力亲为。你的任务是把事情做成、做好、做对、做得称职。很多时候，你所需的资源就掌握在你的上司、伴侣、顾问或导师手中。这些资源就在他们那里。（00:14:25）：作为管理者，我曾无数次遇到这样的情况：有人接到任务后说"我明白了"，然后自行其是，结果却出错。我不会责怪他们的失误——他们没有向我汇报，误解了任务要求，沟通不畅，责任在我。这没关系。（00:14:42）：但六个月后任务仍未达标，就是因为他们误解了任务要求。（00:14:49）：或者耗时一年才完成。我就会问："为什么用了一年而不是六个月？"他们回答："天哪，我有太多杂事缠身。" 其实只要他们发邮件给我，我就能扫清障碍，指明方向。这样就能提前六个月完成任务，他们也会少受许多挫折。这就是所谓的"巧妙干预"。（00:15:09）：作为管理者，我认为我们有责任说："嘿，这就是工作，你得自己想办法解决。" 我常对下属说的最有力的话之一，就是拒绝替他们做决定。比如有人来汇报任务，我们总想插手帮忙。我会说："不必。不过我觉得你能行。你面临的挑战是正确的，处理方式也恰当。尽力而为就好。"这才是关键。作为领导者、导师、顾问或董事会成员，我们也有责任这样做。（00:15:39）：顺便说一句，我们在个人关系中也会这样做。比如和伴侣一起，你想用正确的方式做事，却不和对方沟通。这就是在冒险，却几乎得不到回报。他们不会因为你问"你希望这样做吗？我不太确定"而生气。（00:15:56）：我觉得我们总爱在脑海中构筑堡垒，设置阻碍与外界合作的壁垒，这真的很可笑。昨天我看到一段很棒的引语。帕特里克·斯图尔特（Patrick Stewart）是我最喜欢的演员之一，我很爱他的角色。他谈到演员试镜时说："没人比你试镜的导演更希望你成功，因为他们希望你大放异彩。一旦你成功了，他们的任务就完成了。"
希望你比你的经理更出色，因为当你表现出色时，经理的生活会更轻松，同事的生活也会更轻松。所以，我觉得我们应该抱着这样的心态：“不，不，不。他们是在考验我。”其实不是的。他们是在为你加油。我向你保证这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that advice. I imagine the reason people don't do this, as you said, is they don't want their managers to think they don't know what they're doing, or they can't solve it. Do you have any advice and guidance for when it makes sense to go reach out and ask?
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这个建议。我想，人们不这么做的原因，正如你所说，是不想让经理认为他们不知道自己在做什么，或者无法解决问题。对于何时该主动去寻求帮助，你有什么建议和指导吗？

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: One of the things I think, for people who are timid about this especially, is I think you can put a framing around it that's really easy for your manager to engage with. You can say, "Hey, I'm making progress on this. This is what I'm blocked on, this is the current program." And I'll even say, "Hey, if this all looks good to you, no response required. If there is something here that you want me to do better, different, that you think you could help with, let me know." (00:17:32): I love a typed, five-, 10-sentence email, "No response required. Here's where things are." Even if everything is going really well, I'm like, cool, this person understands the urgency, they understand the assignment, and they're giving me a little heartbeat, a little ping back. (00:17:53): And then also, if two weeks later, let's say the blocking issue is bad, then you say, "Hey, I am sorry, but I do actually need your help now. I'm actually blocked on this thing." I have the context. I have a mental model of you toiling away on the right thing, on the thing I asked you to do over there. Even then, when you're blocked, you can make my life super easy. Like, "Hey, what I'd love for you to do, if you could send an email to this person, here's a draft with this thought, that would help." (00:18:23): Or it's like, here are specific questions framed up. "I think this is what you want. Is this right? Yes or no? If no, okay, we'll come back and we'll spend more time. If yes, we're all good." So now, not only am I up to speed, I have a mental model, I'm engaged. Also, you've made it super cheap for me to help you. And people are always surprised. People who work for me are always surprised when I tell them how big a part of my job is doing these little types of things. (00:18:53): It's a little spinning plates at my scale. I've got 10,000 or 15,000 employees, depending on how you want to count different things. And so, you're just like, every now and then I got to get a whole new plate, a whole new rod, and just really put the effort into it. But for the most part, I'm just trying to touch everything and keep the momentum going. And so, if something falls, and somebody didn't tell me that "Hey, we're losing rotational velocity here. We're losing momentum." Oh, I'm bummed. I'm like, "Ah, now that plate fell. I got to start a whole new thing over here now." (00:19:22): So, I think people underestimate. They think of my job differently than my job actually... My job is actually tons of little touches.
turns.zh: 我认为，尤其是对那些对此有些犹豫的人来说，可以用一种让经理容易接受的方式来处理这个问题。你可以说：“嘿，我在这件事上正在取得进展。这是我遇到的阻碍，目前项目进展情况是这样的。”我甚至会说：“嘿，如果你觉得一切都还好，不需要回复。如果有需要改进的地方，或者你能提供帮助的地方，请告诉我。”（00:17:32）：我喜欢那种五到十句的书面邮件：“无需回复。情况如下。”即使一切进展顺利，我也会想，太棒了，这个人理解紧迫性，理解任务要求，而且还能给我一点反馈，让我安心一点。（00:17:53）：然后，比如说，两周后如果阻碍问题依然严重，你就可以说：“嘿，很抱歉，但我现在确实需要你的帮助了。我在这件事上真的遇到了阻碍。”我已经掌握了上下文，对你正在努力处理正确的事情有了心理预期，即使在遇到阻碍时，你也能让我的工作变得简单。比如，“嘿，如果你能给这个人发封邮件，附上这份带有我思路的草稿，那会很有帮助。”（00:18:23）：或者是一些经过精心组织的具体问题。 “我觉得你想要的是这个。对吗？是还是不是？如果不是，那好，我们再回头花更多时间。如果是，那就没问题了。” 这样一来，我不仅能掌握进展，还能建立心理模型，保持参与感。同时，帮你解决问题也变得容易多了。人们总是很惊讶。为我工作的人总是惊讶于我把这么多精力花在处理这些小事上。 （00:18:53）：对我来说，就是在多个方面同时兼顾。我有1万或1.5万名员工，具体数字取决于你如何统计不同部门。所以，每隔一段时间，我就得拿起新的任务，投入全部精力。但大多数时候，我只是努力关注每个环节，保持势头不减。如果有事情出了差错，有人没告诉我“嘿，我们在这儿失去了动能，失去了势头。”哦，我很失望。我就会想，“啊，这个环节出了问题。现在我得从头再来了。” （00:19:22）：所以，我认为人们低估了这份工作的复杂性。他们对我的工作的理解和实际情况有很大偏差……我的工作实际上就是由无数个小细节组成的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, I think a key takeaway here is, one, index more towards asking your manager and leaders for help. And I love this way of framing it of, it doesn't always need to be like, "Here's what I need from you." It's, "Here's what's happening. Here's things that might be blocking me. Here's questions I have. Here's things that are going on." (00:19:44): This is actually similar to something I found really powerful that I'll share real quickly, this idea of a state of... I call it the State of Lenny email. And I sent this email to my manager every week. The State of Lenny. It's kind of like State of the Union. And it's, "Here's my current priorities, here's what's on my mind broadly, and then here's blockers that I need your help with.
turns.zh: 因此，我认为一个关键的收获是，首先，要更主动地向你的经理和领导寻求帮助。我特别喜欢用这种方式来表达：不必总是说"我需要你帮我做什么"，而是可以说："这是正在发生的情况。这些因素可能阻碍了我。这些问题我需要你的帮助。" （00:19:44）：这其实和我发现的一个非常有效的方法很相似，我很快就和大家分享一下——我称之为"Lenny状态报告"的邮件。我每周都会把这封邮件发给我的经理，名为"Lenny状态报告"。它有点像"国情咨文"。内容包括：我当前的优先事项、我对大局的看法，以及需要你帮助解决的阻碍问题。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: We actually used to have a format for that we called HPMs. Highlight, people, me. And every manager at Facebook from like 2008 to like 2014 would send to their manager, or even their leadership group. I mean, at one point when I was running what we called comm apps, I just sent it to Zuck and the whole leadership group. (00:20:24): It's like, what's the highlights include? And it highlights [inaudible 00:20:27] flow. What's the big ticket things you need to know? Where are people? Like is somebody in trouble? Is somebody at risk? Is somebody doing really amazing work that needs a shout-out? And then me, how are you personally doing? HPMs, we called them. (00:20:39): Actually, it's funny. I hadn't thought about that in a long time. But yeah, no, I think this kind of thing can work. And look, every manager is different, so even at the Meta level, by the way, is another success. I think what people do is they want to treat every manager the same, and that's not going to work because every manager is different. (00:20:54): But every manager, you can ask, "How do you like to get updates?" You can ask them when you first start working with them. Like, "Hey, what's your cadence? How do you like to stay informed?" And so, for me, I do regular one-on-ones. As the org's has gotten bigger, those have gotten more distant, so people have replaced those with more written things. (00:21:11): But no manager will get pissed at you if you're like, "How do you like to get information about me?" That's a totally reasonable thing to ask.
turns.zh: 我们过去曾为此制定了一个格式，叫做HPMs（Highlight, People, Me）。从2008年到2014年，Facebook的每位经理都会把这份报告发送给他们的上级，甚至整个领导团队。比如，当我负责通讯应用部门时，我会直接发送给扎克伯格和整个领导团队。（00:20:24）：HPMs的内容包括什么？它会突出[00:20:27]进展情况。你需要他们知道的重大事项有哪些？团队成员的情况如何？比如是否有人遇到麻烦？是否有人面临风险？是否有人工作表现出色，值得表扬？然后是关于我个人情况的部分，HPMs就是这么命名的。（00:20:39）：说真的，我已经很久没想起这个了。但没错，我认为这种方法确实有效。当然，每位经理都不同，就拿Meta公司来说，他们在这方面也取得了成功。我觉得人们往往想把每位经理都一视同仁，但这行不通，因为每位经理都各不相同。（00:20:54）：但每位经理都不会因为你问"你希望如何获取我的最新动态"而生气。这是一个完全合理的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love the specific idea you shared of just drafting the email to say the other team leader, "Here's what I need you to tell them. That would really unblock this thing." And that's such a cool idea.
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢你分享的具体做法——直接起草邮件告诉另一位团队领导："这是我需要你转达给他们的内容。"这真是个很棒的主意。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: By the way, I always put my own... I don't take that copy paste it. I'm always looking at that and be like, "Okay, I understand." A lot of it is actually not about what you want the other person to hear, it's about the voice, the tone. (00:21:41): It includes a lot of history. I don't know. Have you been going back and forth with them for 12 rounds, and this is going to feel to them like I'm really coming over the top? Or is this like, "Hey, first time you're hearing about this, my bad. Here's what we're doing. Need your help." (00:21:54): So, a lot of that isn't even about making my life easy because I want to copy paste. A lot of it is, actually, there's a rich set of information in how you tone and how you draft that note that's going to help me land it correctly and not feel like I'm just out of band, heavy coming in.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，我从不直接复制粘贴现有内容。我总是通读一遍，思考："好的，我理解了。"很多内容其实不是关于你想让对方听到什么，而是语气和风格。（00:21:41）：邮件中包含大量历史背景。我不知道。你是否和他们反复沟通了12轮，而这封邮件对他们来说会感觉我是在强行插话？还是像"嘿，这是你第一次听说这件事，对不起。以下是我们的计划，需要你的帮助。"（00:21:54）：所以，很多时候这甚至不是为了让自己的工作更轻松，因为我不想复制粘贴。实际上，邮件的语气和格式中蕴含着丰富的信息，这能帮助我准确传达信息，而不会让人觉得我是在越界、强行插话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This touches on something that I often hear is very core to the way Meta works, which is transparency. Anyone can ask Zuck questions at the Q&A's. People are encouraged to post constantly internally of what they're thinking, what they're working on. All the data is shared publicly. Which often leads to leaks, which I hear you hate, and that is a pet peeve of yours.
turns.zh: 这让我想起一个我常听到的理念，它是Meta公司运作方式的核心——透明度。任何人都可以在问答环节向扎克伯格提问。公司鼓励员工不断在内部平台上分享自己的想法和工作进展，所有数据都公开共享。这往往会导致信息泄露，而我听说你对此深恶痛疾。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Just feels like a violation of the team trust. Just feels like... I grew up with playing sports, right? I was football, soccer, track. And you just can't imagine one of your guys calling out the play to the other team. Can you imagine what you would do in that case? "You're off the team. I'm sorry, you can't be here." Anyways, sorry. Carry on.
turns.zh: 这感觉像是对团队信任的背叛。就拿我打球的经历来说吧——我打过橄榄球、足球、田径赛事。你根本无法想象队友会把战术透露给对手。你能想象那种情况下教练会怎么做吗？“你被开除了。很抱歉，你不能继续留队了。” 总之，抱歉打断。继续吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, and there's so many more people, it's hard to find. Who is this? So, with this downside as an example, and I imagine there's other downsides also takes a lot of work, and it puts people on the spot a lot of times, what have you seen as benefits and why is that such a big part of Meta's way of working?
turns.zh: 是啊，还有太多人了，很难找到。谁是这个人？以这个负面例子为例，我相信还有其他负面影响。这需要付出巨大努力，还经常让员工处于被迫的境地。你认为有什么好处呢？为什么透明度在Meta的工作方式中占据如此重要的地位？

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Yeah. This kind of comes back to, I think, the principle that really good, talented people, you want to leverage them fully. You really want to make sure that they are fully leveraged. And so, anytime they have the wrong information, or they don't have the information, you've now blocked one of the economically most valuable things that your company possesses, which is this person's time, attention, talent. Not only that, you've also made them more frustrated, and now they are more likely to leave. (00:23:35): If the lifeblood of any company are the people inside of it who collectively commit to some kind of a goal and a mission and work together, then you want to maximize that potential. And creating this really open information ecosystem is one of the ways that we do that. So often, great, phenomenal work that has happened at our company has not come from this one top-down mandate, but has come from people understanding not just what we're trying to accomplish top down, but also having way more information at their disposal to be able to act on it. (00:24:16): People talk about top-down or bottoms-up culture, and it's a bit of a myth, in my opinion. If you've ever met Mark Zuckerberg, it's not a bottoms-up thing. The ideas that we're pursuing are Mark Zuckerberg's ideas, first and foremost. That's not to say that he's not open to new ones, and of course he is, and that's a form of bottom-up, people can bring ideas to him and he internalizes them and acts them or not. But when he brings things top-down, he's not micromanaging, he's in the details. I'll be careful on that. (00:24:44): But he does create the space for you to bring back three or four versions of the thing that he's talking about, and then he shapes it from there. And you can't do that if there's... If you don't have degrees of freedom, sure, but also if you don't have the information. Otherwise, if you don't have the information available, what we're trying to accomplish, why we're trying to do it, what the infrastructure is like, what the availability is like, what the performance is going to be like, well, you just are stuck. You're just going to have to follow the script. That's very boring for high-talent, high-creativity, high-engaged people. (00:25:15): Now, it does come at a tremendous price. You have to get really good at managing information on the incoming. Most people at most companies consume all the information that's given to them, but the information itself is carefully managed. They're getting all the information they're intended to get. (00:25:32): We've turned that on its head, and it sounds great, but it's not free. Even somebody senior coming from outside of the company to the company, one of the things I have to coach them on is, how do you find signal amongst all the noise? (00:25:45): You have to have a system for managing your information. You have to have a system for triaging the incoming, getting rid of a bunch of stuff that is on the wrong channel, or it doesn't matter to you, figuring out what's the... groups that you want to be a part of, but you consume only when you choose to and-
turns.zh:
是的。这归根结底在于，我认为真正优秀、有才华的人才需要被充分利用。你必须确保他们能充分发挥潜力。所以，一旦他们获取了错误的信息，或者根本没有信息可用，你就阻断了公司最具经济价值的资源——即这些人才的时间、注意力和才能。不仅如此，这还会让他们更加沮丧，从而增加离职的可能性。

（00:23:35）：如果说任何公司的命脉都是内部员工，他们共同致力于某个目标并携手合作，那么你就需要最大限度地挖掘他们的潜力。创建一个真正开放的信息生态系统，就是实现这一目标的途径之一。在我们公司，许多伟大的、非凡的工作成果并非源于自上而下的强制要求，而是源于员工不仅理解了公司自上而下设定的目标，还能获取更多信息并据此采取行动。

（00:24:16）：人们常谈论自上而下或自下而上的文化，但在我看来这不过是种神话。如果你见过马克·扎克伯格，就会发现这根本不是自下而上的模式。我们所追求的理念首先是马克·扎克伯格的构想。这并不是说他不接受新想法——他当然乐于倾听——这就是自下而上的形式，员工可以向他提出想法，他会考虑并采取行动。但当他自上而下地提出方案时，他并非在微观管理，而是在关注细节。我得小心措辞。

（00:24:44）：但他确实为你创造了空间，让你能就他提出的想法提出三四个版本，然后他再从中进行塑造。如果没有自由度空间，或者缺乏信息获取渠道，那就无法做到这一点。否则，如果没有信息支持——我们要达成的目标、达成目标的路径、基础设施现状、可用性如何、性能表现如何——那就只能按部就班。这对高才能、高创造力、高敬业度的人来说实在无趣。

（00:25:15）：当然，这需要付出巨大代价。你必须善于管理输入信息。大多数公司员工都会接收所有提供的信息，但这些信息本身是经过精心管理的。他们只获取了预期获取的信息。

（00:25:32）：我们彻底颠覆了这一模式，听起来很棒，但并非免费。即使是从外部加入公司的资深人士，我也必须指导他们如何在众多噪音中捕捉信号。

（00:25:45）：你必须建立信息管理体系。必须建立信息分类机制，筛选掉错误信息或无关信息，明确你想加入的群体，并仅在自愿情况下获取信息。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: ... groups that you want to be a part of but you consume only when you choose to. And where are the things where you're getting push notice? Like that's the real time thing, and that takes some time.
turns.zh: ……以及你想加入的群体，但你只在自愿情况下获取信息。还有哪些信息会推送通知？这才是实时信息，而这需要时间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This point you made about bottom up versus top down is really interesting, because, when I think of Meta, I think it's a very bottom up culture. I hear everyone comes up with their ideas, runs experiments, is very encouraged to just try stuff, and it's really interesting to hear that. And it makes a lot of sense that most of the big ideas actually do come from the top.
turns.zh: 您提到的自下而上与自上而下的观点确实很有趣，因为一想到Meta，我就觉得它是一种非常强调自下而上的文化。我听说每个人都能提出自己的想法，开展实验，公司非常鼓励大家去尝试新事物。听到这些真的很有意思。同时，大多数重大创意确实来自高层管理层，这一点也说得通。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: It's of these mythology things. I don't think it's the wrong... As a contract, it's more bottoms up than many other companies, because you do have these degrees of freedom within the construct. But make no mistake, like Mark or me or Chris Cox or Javi, they have very strong opinions about what we should be doing as a company, and your bottoms up-ness works within that framework. But it is true that you can ask Mark any question, and he's going to answer it. Same with me, same with Chris, same with Javi and also that we certainly take inspiration from the discussion that we have with employees. So I don't know, it's just not as black and white as people tend to paint it.
turns.zh: 这涉及到一些企业文化的误解。我不认为这有什么错……作为一家公司，Meta比许多其他公司更具自下而上的文化，因为公司架构内确实有一定程度的自由度。但别误会，像马克、我、克里斯·考克斯或哈维，他们对公司的战略方向都有非常明确的看法，而自下而上的文化也必须在这种框架内运作。但确实，你可以向马克提出任何问题，他都会回答。对我也是如此，对克里斯和哈维也是如此。此外，我们也确实从与员工的讨论中获得灵感。所以我觉得这并非人们想象中非黑即白的二元对立。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think one of the biggest lessons here is making it at least feel like you have a lot of say, even though a company is very, "Here's the big strategic [inaudible 00:27:10]," you're very good at making people feel like they can have an impact and a say.
turns.zh: 我认为最重要的经验是，让员工至少感觉自己有很大的发言权，即便公司会说“这是重大战略决策”之类的话，但你要善于让员工感受到自己的影响力和发言权。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: And can I tell you, the most important thing is just giving people clear guidelines so they know where they... Like, "Where do they have space and where do they have no space?" One of the things that we go in these reviews with Mark or my team with me I'm sure, and I'm like, "For this part of the UI, it is going to... Like, I will draw it for you. It's going to be like this." And this other part. I'm like, "Cool, that's important, too. I don't have a clear vision of it. Why don't you do it?" So there's just really clear guardrails of like, "Okay, where are we just on assignment? And where do we have more flexibility?"
turns.zh: 我可以告诉你，最重要的是给员工明确的指导方针，让他们清楚自己的权限范围。比如，“在UI的这个部分，你有自由发挥的空间；在另一个部分，你没有自由发挥的空间。”在与马克或我的团队进行评审时，我会明确说明：“对于UI的这部分，我会为你画出设计草案。它应该这样做。”而对于另一部分，我会说：“不错，这也很重要。但我对此没有清晰的构想。你来负责吧。”所以，我们设有非常清晰的界限，明确区分“哪些是必须遵循的任务，哪些有更大的灵活性”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example of that that comes to mind where you were just very in the details and drawing the screen?
turns.zh: 您能举个例子说明您是如何深入到细节层面、亲自绘制屏幕设计的吗？

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Over the course of time, there's been quite a few examples. I think early on, when we were working on News Feed, mark was absolutely whiteboarding every single pixel that the team had to put on the front end. On the back end, he was like, "Make it rank, have some ranking." So I felt like I was lucky there. I was just like, "Cool, I'm off to the races on some ranking stuff." And Chris Cox and all these other guys are having to really pixel-match these things. But it's not always that way by the way. So now fast-forward and we're talking about ranking, it's not like Mark is always hands-off on that. When we got into modernizing our ranking systems, which we've done over the last five years, Mark was heavily involved and like, " Hey, what's the mix shift and how are you weighing different things?" (00:28:33): And so it can go both ways. For me personally, I've gotten really involved in some relatively esoteric things. I was really adamant, for example, that hand tracking and mixed reality make it into the headset. Let's just say that there weren't any supporters in the team. Obviously we had a hand tracking team, which is phenomenal, mixed reality team, but there was a lot of people who were like... They did not feel those features were going to be critical for this to become a mainstream device. I always believed that they were for ease of use and for... So I just really forced the issue and didn't give anyone any room and held really high standards for the performance benchmarks we were going to hit on the hand tracking. And teams told me it was impossible. And it wasn't. It did great.
turns.zh: 长久以来，这样的例子屡见不鲜。我记得早期我们开发News Feed时，马克简直在白板上把团队需要在前端呈现的每个像素都一一标注出来。在后端，他则会强调：“要让排序机制发挥作用，做好排名优化。” 所以我觉得自己当时很幸运。我当时就想：“太棒了，我要全力推进排名优化了。” 而克里斯·考克斯等其他团队成员却不得不逐像素地去匹配各种需求。不过，情况并非一直如此。快进到现在，我们再谈论排名优化时，马克也并非总是置身事外。过去五年里，我们在现代化排名系统上投入巨大时，马克深度参与其中，反复追问：“混合模型占比如何？不同因素的权重又是怎么设定的？” （00:28:33） 可见，事情的两面性很明显。就我个人而言，我曾深度参与一些相对冷门的技术研发。比如，我坚信手部追踪和混合现实技术必须要加入头显设备。只不过当时团队里没人支持这个想法。虽然我们有出色的手部追踪团队和混合现实团队，但许多人认为这些功能对主流设备来说并非关键。我始终坚信它们能提升易用性，因此我坚持己见，不给任何人退路，对手部追踪的性能基准要求极高。团队告诉我这根本不可能，但结果证明我做到了——效果非常出色。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This touches on something that comes up a lot on this podcast. And there's this debate between how in-the-weeds founders and execs should be, whether they delegate, empower, versus, "No, we're just going to do it this way. I'm going to be very involved in every mock." And there's always this up and down that happens where it's like, "Okay, cool, we're going to let people run and do their thing," and then things start to not work as well often. And then, "We're going to take back control." You have just a perspective on when it makes sense to go deep, how founders execs should think about that?
turns.zh: 这正触及了播客中反复出现的一个话题。关于创始人和高管该如何深入参与细节，是放权授权，还是亲力亲为？有时会出现反复的拉锯战：先是放手让团队自由发挥，后来发现效果不佳，又重新收回控制权。您能否谈谈何时该深度参与，创始人和高管该如何看待这个问题？

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Such a useless answer for founders, it depends on the weeds. There are some weeds that really matter and there's some weeds that really just don't, and I should say, that doesn't mean they don't matter at all. You have to do them, but they aren't the hinge upon which success or failure will happen. Yeah, there's people I really respect, Brian Chesky's been on and said, "Look, the Airbnb is going to work only on the things that I can work on. It's that's the extent of what it's going to do." And that's a super extreme form of it. I have a lot of respect for him and how they're working things. I think that if you have great super talented people that you can trust who can own bigger pieces, that's one option. If there are ways to structure it so that you can check in effectively and make sure that it's on track, that's another way to structure it. (00:30:27): And there probably is still work happening at Airbnb, that has to happen, finance and accounting and HR, that Brian isn't personally managing. So there are clearly non-technical areas that we do. Or legal. There are areas that we do trust that this is happening at. And so I think a lot of founders regret delegating too much, from my conversations. And I totally get that. Or they delegated something critical that really turned out to be the most important thing. For me, the judgment is like, "How do you, most important, determine what is what matters the most?" And so Mark, we joke inside of Meta, to this day, we call it the eye of Sauron. When Mark has determined that the thing that you're working on is the most important thing, there is no detail too small for him to notice. (00:31:17): He will be in a review, and in the same review. We'll be like, "Strategically, I think we're off course. And also, this one pixel is definitely wrong. You have to fix that." That's a big range. Frankly, I'll be a little bit self-congratulatory, I pride myself on being able to do the same. And I think people who work with me often comment that the style of leadership that we have, and I think Chris Cox is the same, is where it's like we will go where hide a low on the things that matter a ton. And there's a bunch of other things that certainly matter. We're glad we're doing them, but either they have pretty clear roadmaps, pretty clear examples in the industry, or it's like that's a feature that you have to have but isn't going to determine success or failure. So getting it into rough shape and then iterating on it is fine. And so I think it really does depend on the weeds, how deep you want to get.
turns.zh: 这种回答对创业者来说太没用了，关键在于区分哪些事务是重要的，哪些只是无关紧要的。当然，这并不意味着它们毫无意义。你必须处理这些事务，但它们并非决定成败的关键。是啊，我很敬重布莱恩·切斯基，他曾说过：“Airbnb只会专注于我能亲自操盘的业务，仅此而已。” 这是一种极端的做法。我非常尊重他和他的团队。我认为，如果你有才华横溢、值得信赖、能够独当一面的核心团队，这是一个可行的选择。如果能通过合理的架构设计，确保项目有效推进，这也是一种有效的管理方式。（00:30:27）Airbnb显然仍在处理一些非技术性工作，比如财务、会计和人力资源，这些都不是布莱恩亲自管理的。所以我们确实在处理一些非技术领域的事务，比如法律事务。有些领域我们确实放权了，但这些领域的进展我们也会密切关注。从我与许多创业者的交流来看，他们都后悔过授权过多。我完全理解这种心理。或者他们把一些关键任务授权出去，结果发现那恰恰是最重要的。对我来说，关键在于如何判断什么是最重要的。在Meta内部，我们开玩笑称这为“索伦之眼”。当马克认定你正在做的事情是最重要的，那么再细微的细节他都会注意到。他会在评审会上指出：“从战略角度看，我们偏离了轨道。”同时，他也会指出：“这一个像素有问题，你必须改正。” 这种要求极高的标准，坦白说，我也会自我激励，我为自己能做到这一点而自豪。我想和我共事的人也经常评论，我们和克里斯·考克斯领导风格相似，就是那种对关键事务全力以赴，对其他事务则保持适度关注。当然，还有很多其他重要的事务。我们很高兴能做这些事，但要么它们有明确的路线图，要么在行业内有成功案例，要么就是必须具备但不会决定成败的功能。所以先把框架搭好，然后逐步完善就足够了。所以我认为关键还是在于区分主次，要知道什么时候该深入，什么时候该适可而止。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's so funny, I use exactly that same metaphor, the eye of Sauron, when I talk about working on things that Airbnb that matter a lot to Brian. And my advice to people is, "You don't want to be in that eye of Sauron for too long in your career, because you're just going to burn out if you're working on the most important thing all the time, but want to be close. You don't want to be in the Shire, but you want to be around the [inaudible 00:32:26].
turns.zh: 有趣的是，我在谈论Airbnb对布莱恩来说重要的事情时，也会用索伦之眼这个比喻。我给人们的建议是：“你不希望在职业生涯中长时间处于索伦之眼的注视下，因为如果你一直专注于最重要的事情，却又想保持亲力亲为，最终会精疲力竭。但你又不甘心置身于夏尔王国（指平凡生活），而想在迷雾山脉（指挑战）附近。”

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: That's right. They're both... So I worked for years in ads. From 2012 to 2017, I ran ads in a business platform, this big ads group, and it was an area where certainly it was very important, but Mark had so many other things going on with the transition to mobile, he did kind of delegate it to me. And it was awesome, and it was so cool to have that kind of trust from him. And also, you're constantly terrified, because like, "Mark does not know. What if this is all..." My leads would be worried, because they just hadn't had a review with Mark in a while. And it's like, yeah, you suffer in the intensity of the gaze of Sauron. You also suffer in the shadow of its absence. There's no perfect place to be.
turns.zh: 没错。它们都是……所以我在广告领域工作了多年。从2012年到2017年，我在一个商业平台上负责广告业务，这个大型广告团队所在的部门固然很重要，但马克当时正忙于向移动端转型，所以他把这部分工作交给了我。这段经历棒极了，能得到他的信任真是太好了。不过你也会时刻感到压力重重——比如，“马克不了解情况。要是这事搞砸了……”我的下属们也很焦虑，因为他们已经很久没得到马克的审核了。这就好比，嗯，你既要承受索隆目光的审视，又要忍受他缺席的阴影。没有一个完美境地。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's hilarious. I'm trying to think of the part of Middle Earth that is a metaphor for that.
turns.zh: 太逗了。我正想找个中土世界的片段来比喻这种情况呢。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so you talked about the News Feed, which was one of your very earliest projects at Facebook. Here's a couple fun facts I know about the News Feed. One is that it was the very first algorithmic News Feed of its kind of any social network and maybe of any sort of product like this. And two, it was the very first AI code that was written at Facebook to rank the actual News Feed. So there were a lot of firsts, and clearly this became a huge deal. The News Feed is essentially what people think of when they think of Facebook now, but it was super controversial when it came out. People were very against this. They did not want to be sharing this much information with people, or so they thought, and then they realized eventually, "Oh, this is actually exactly what I want." What did you learn from going through that experience of building something that people initially reject and then later realize that they actually do want this and this is exactly what they're waiting for?
turns.zh: 好的，你提到了News Feed，这是你在Facebook最早参与的项目之一。关于News Feed，我了解几个趣事。其一，它是首个社交网络或类似产品中采用算法推荐的News Feed。其二，它是Facebook编写的首个用于News Feed排序的人工智能代码。可见这里有很多开创性成果，而News Feed最终也成了Facebook的核心产品。但它推出时引发了巨大争议，很多人反对，担心信息泄露过多。后来用户逐渐意识到：“这正是我们想要的！”从打造这款最初遭人排斥、后来被认可的产品的经历中，你收获了什么？

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: This is a story that you tell a lot actually through your interviews, which is just like, "You have to have conviction in what you're building." You're choosing your customers as much as your customers are choosing you, is one way I think about it sometimes, and one mistake that you do see sometimes startups make is they get an early cohort of users whose needs actually take them kind of orthogonal to a larger market. And so they become kind of held hostage by their earliest customers now. So time and time again, we've had a vision for what we thought this should look like, and it wasn't the thing we were delivering right now. And so people who were using the thing we currently had were not sure that that change was what they wanted. But we had a confidence that over time they would, and we're not always right, but in these cases we were right. Now News Feed was an easier case than people suspect, because everyone was outraged at the same time as they immediately doubled their usage of the product. (00:35:05): So we had a few advantages there, which was, it was literally like everyone was like, "I hate this so much." And they would refresh, refresh, refresh. And so we were like, Okay, wait, there's cognitive dissonance here between what the stated preferences and what the revealed preferences are in the economic sense. So News Feed was a little easier than people suspect, to us, to stick with. But people sometimes misunderstand that. They think, "Oh, the lesson is don't listen to your customers. Not at all." And we certainly care a tremendous amount. And even with News Feed, we did actually screw some things up. I kind of always make this joke that it's almost like... You know when you're at the party and music's loud, you're talking to somebody and the music cuts out right when you're saying something at a super high volume, and so everyone in the party hears the last thing you said? (00:35:42): Now you were saying it in a public place, so it wasn't like it was a private comment, but you also didn't mean to broadcast it at that volume. We kind of did that to the entire user base. We took what had been wall posts, which sure, anybody could have gone to that profile and seen and then put it kind of on blast, on Main, as the kids say these days, "Put it on Main," and someone's like, "Ah." So we did that. I don't want to say it like... We did screw things up. It wasn't like, "Oh, this is a clause execution." So another thing to know is like, "When did you screw something small up, and when did you do something big up?" When is the thing itself wrong, versus when were the details wrong? That is an art. That is a real art, and you don't always have user data to determine it like we did. (00:36:25): And so a lot of that is, "Do you have a clear vision and intuition for what you expected to happen?" And then what happened instead and can you diagnose the delta there? So in the News Feed case, we made a bunch of little mistakes. The thing itself was right, and I really am quite proud of the work we did there. Me and Chris Cox at the most core probably in the engineering side, which you saw as the PM, there was no ranked feeds before that. We did have some AI that I built before for the anti-spam, anti... things, but it was pretty rudimentary, but it was probably the first consumer AI that was in a website of that kind around content. And we built the most efficient monetizing surface in history outside of Search, I think. [inaudible 00:37:04] for those who are curious, I don't use monetization because I think money's the most important thing. I do think it suggests the economic power you've created, which I do think correlates very strongly with human utility. Although obviously I respect that some people may disagree.
turns.zh:
实际上，在采访中你经常提到这个观点："你必须对自己正在打造的东西充满信心。"我有时会这样理解：选择客户和被客户选择同样重要。有时候初创公司会犯的一个错误是，他们获取的早期用户群体需求与更广阔市场需求方向相背离，最终被早期客户"挟持"。一次又一次，我们对产品的设想与实际交付的成果存在偏差。使用现有产品的用户不确定这样的改进是否符合他们的需求，但我们坚信随着时间推移他们会接受。事实证明，我们的判断没错。

News Feed的案例比人们想象的要容易得多，因为当所有人都对其反感时，用户使用量反而翻倍。我们利用了这种认知失调——用户口口声声说讨厌某个功能，却不断刷新页面。这让我们意识到，用户的表态与真实需求存在巨大落差。News Feed之所以能坚持下去，关键在于我们从不忽视用户意见。即便在News Feed项目中，我们也确实犯过错。我常打比方：当你在派对上大声说话时，音乐突然停掉，所有人听到你最后那句话。虽然你本意不是要公开，但结果却被全网传播。我们把原本私密的墙贴内容公开化，让用户能在主页上分享。这次失误并非策略性错误，而是细节处理不当。如何判断是产品本身有问题，还是执行细节出错？这是一门艺术，需要敏锐的洞察力和用户数据支持。

（00:36:25）在News Feed案例中，我们犯了诸多小错误，但核心功能无可指摘。我为团队的成果深感自豪。最核心的工程团队由Chris Cox和我负责。在此之前，News Feed没有排名机制。我们开发的反垃圾邮件AI虽然初级，但可能是当时首个基于内容的消费级AI。除搜索外，我们打造了史上最高效的变现平台。[00:37:04不可听清]好奇的朋友，我不参与变现业务，因为我认为金钱是最不重要的因素。
嗯，我确实认为这反映了你所创造的经济价值，而我认为这与人类的效用有着非常紧密的关联。不过显然，我尊重有些人可能对此持不同意见。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In terms of the economic utility, the Venn diagram of Boz, of News Feed and ads, create $1 trillion dollars of value.
turns.zh: 就经济效益而言，博兹（Boz）提出的新闻推送与广告的维恩图，能创造出价值1万亿美元的价值。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: It's not-
turns.zh: 这可不是——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well done.
turns.zh: 干得好。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: It's not nothing, not nothing.
turns.zh: 这可不是小事，不是小事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: [inaudible 00:37:27].

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: We're proud of that work.
turns.zh: 我们为此感到自豪。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You have this quote in one of your posts about the News Feed where you said, "It consumed me more fully than anything in life had ever consumed me. It opened up to me the truth that when you're passionate about something, you do better work, you do smarter work and you're, in order of magnitude, more productive."
turns.zh: 你在关于News Feed的帖子中提到过这句话："它比我人生中任何事物都更能占据我的心思。它让我领悟到，当你对某件事充满热情时，你会做出更出色的工作，更明智的决策，效率也会显著提升。"

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: There's no substitute for it. One thing I've learned about myself since that post actually is just the degree to which I am somebody who is inclined to be passionate about things. And it's a gift that I'm lucky to have, and I understand that's not every person. And so actually the ads thing is a good example. When Mark told me to go work on ads, I was like, " No, I don't want to. I don't think I have a passion for that." I had this idea of myself. I had a very strong identity of myself as this AI infrastructure product guy, and I was working in this space and nope, I was wrong. I just am a guy who gets excited about things. Once I get into ads, it's like, "Oh, this is fascinating. It's a three-sided marketplace, and there's all these different..." It felt like I was playing chess times in terms of the moves with the other players in the industry, and I was super pumped about that. (00:38:26): And then when he wanted me to work on hardware, I was like, "No, I'm not. I'm a software guy. I'm a software guy, Mark." And now, I love this work. That's such a fascinating space that I've learned so much. So I do think that's right. I do think what I find something I'm passionate about that's good. What I have learned since then is to give myself a space to understand if I can get passionate about it. Now, there are parts of jobs that I've had before where I just never found the passion, and after six months I just have to move on. Literally it's like I'll either quit, get fired, I'm doing bad work, I don't care about the work. And so I do have a self-awareness. It's not that I can get passionate about anything, but I do have a pretty broad palette, it turns out.
turns.zh: 没有什么能替代它。自那篇帖子以来，我对自己有了更深刻的认识——我天生就容易对事物充满热情。这是上天赐予我的礼物，并非每个人都能拥有。拿广告业务来说吧，当马克让我去负责广告项目时，我当时就说："不，我不想做。我对这件事没热情。"我对自己的定位很清晰，深信自己是AI基础设施领域的专家。但事实证明，我错了。我其实是个容易为新事物兴奋的人。接触广告业务后，我发现这是一个三方市场，里面充满了各种挑战……这就像在棋盘上与业界对手博弈，我对此乐此不疲。（00:38:26）后来马克想让我负责硬件项目时，我又说："不行，我不行。马克，我是软件工程师。"但现在我爱上了这份工作。这是一个让我收获满满的迷人领域。所以我确实认同这句话。我认为找到自己热爱的事物是件好事。自那以后我学到，要给自己时间去判断能否对某件事产生热情。过去有些工作我始终找不到热情，六个月后只能选择离开。说白了，要么辞职，要么被裁，要么工作质量太差，要么根本不在乎。可见我对自我的认知还挺清晰的。并非什么事都能让我充满热情，但事实证明，我的兴趣范围还挺广。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think that's a really interesting career lesson of, "Don't assume you won't be excited about something that may come up." Is there anything there that you'd share with folks of just like, "Explore it, give it six months, see if you can get excited about it?"
turns.zh: 我觉得这是一个很有启发的职业经验："别想当然地认为自己对即将面临的新事物会毫无热情。" 你能否给出一些建议，比如："去探索一下，坚持六个月，看看能否激发热情？"

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Absolutely. So I have a very unusual career arc in some ways, which is I really almost changed jobs every six months for a long time. I was working on this integrity stuff with News Feed in the background. Then I was working on News Feed for about a year. Then I worked on site speed and infrastructure and detecting SAVs and issues. And then I worked on Bootcamp, and then I worked on messaging and groups. I had this really funny thing. I was kind of joking it was like, for those who are old enough to remember Karate Kid, I felt like I was painting a lot of fences, waxing a lot of cars, and at the end I knew karate. I was like at the end, at the end I had the payoff, because I'd gone through and I'd met a lot of people and I'd worked in these different areas and I understood different dynamics. Well, other people who joined in my cohort were getting promoted, but they were in a single track. They just stayed in one place and they got promoted, whereas I kept moving around. And it probably at some point early in my career felt like I was moving more slowly relative to my peers. And then when I finally turned the corner, really with the ads appointment, which I did for five years, I went vertical. I just like my career went vertical. And since then I've kind of been on that trajectory. And so advice I most often give people, for me at least, the lesson that I take from this, is I just was willing to learn aggressively. I would move because I wasn't learning enough. I was bored, and so I wasn't learning enough new stuff. And what was cool about finally getting to the ads job, and likewise in the job I'm in now, is those jobs, I learned a ton for five years. I'd never stopped learning in those jobs. You will occasionally find those jobs where they're super deep and you can just keep learning. (00:40:50): Meanwhile, a lot of my friends whose careers were on a better trajectory [inaudible 00:40:55] then earlier, they literally got bored of what they were doing, but they didn't have any place to jump to. There wasn't some other... They'd become domain specialists in a domain that they'd kind of exhausted for themselves. And maybe they'd even stuck around longer than they wanted to because it was comfortable or because the company wanted them to. And it ended up kind of being a hindrance to them in the middle of their career. And so for me, it's like, "Jump into new things, give it six months. If it's not the thing, no problem. You just built a ton of new skills that's going to come in handy, I promise you that. Keep going." And likewise, when you do make that jump early career, optimize for learning, optimize for... Think about a compound interest. It's like the first 10 years of compound interest don't look that impressive. It's like after 10 years it starts to look good.
turns.zh:
没错。所以我的职业生涯轨迹在某些方面相当不寻常——很长一段时间里，我几乎每六个月就换一份工作。起初，我专注于新闻推送的诚信问题，同时兼顾其他业务。后来，我在新闻推送团队工作了大约一年。接着，我转去做站点速度和基础设施优化，以及SAV（安全漏洞）检测。再后来，我参与了Bootcamp项目，之后又负责了消息和群组功能。说来挺有趣的，我常开玩笑说，这就像《龙威小子》里的场景——我四处修补关系、擦车，最后才掌握了真功夫。到最后，我才获得了回报——积累了丰富经验，结识了各路人物，深刻理解了不同领域的运作机制。与同期入职的同事相比，我晋升得较慢。但当我最终迎来转机——接手广告业务并深耕五年后——我的职业生涯便直线攀升。此后，我便始终保持着这种发展轨迹。给别人的建议呢？对我个人而言，最重要的启示就是保持积极学习的态度。若某个岗位学不到新东西，我就勇于跳槽。同样，在现职岗位上，我也始终保持着这种学习习惯。偶尔也会遇到能深度钻研的职位，但五年内都能收获满满。

（00:40:50）与此同时，我很多朋友的职业发展轨迹本应更顺畅，却最终陷入困境。他们对现有工作失去兴趣，却找不到跳槽的出路。要么深耕某个领域却已探索殆尽，要么因为安逸或公司要求而被困原地。这种职业停滞最终成了他们职业生涯中期的一大阻碍。

对我来说，关键在于：“勇于尝试新事物，坚持六个月。如果不合适，再调整。这些新技能迟早会派上用场，相信我。继续前进。” 同样，早期跳槽时也要优化学习路径，效仿复利效应。前十年看似平淡无奇，但十年后成果斐然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that advice. It's similar advice I always give of, "Variety of experience often ends up being the most valuable thing you build over time," just trying to bunch of stuff, doing some internal tools, maybe working on customer support, I don't know, trust and safety, user-facing products, infrastructure. I'm thinking from a PM's perspective, maybe an engineers, and other functions. One question along those lines. So we talked about the eye of Sauron and working on the most important thing at the company. Do you have any advice on how much of your career you should be working in that center?
turns.zh: 我很赞同这种建议。这和我常给出的忠告如出一辙：“多元化经验往往是职业生涯中最宝贵的财富。” 比如尝试内部工具开发、客户支持、信任与安全、面向用户的产品、基础设施建设等。我从产品经理、工程师及其他职能的角度来思考这个问题。有个相关问题：我们之前谈到“索伦之眼”（指公司最核心的任务），您对职业生涯中应如何专注于这类核心工作有什么建议？

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Yeah, listen, [inaudible 00:42:12] being equal, I think there's two really good places to be. I think one is carrying a lot of water in areas that the company's not paying attention to but you are important. And it needs to be a lot. You got to own that stuff and really move mountains over there, because I promise you, as an executive, when there's a huge dam holding up the floodwaters, you respect the heck out of the person who is holding that dam up. You're like, "You keep doing that, Atlas, that is good work over there." The second-best place to be, or maybe equally, is on the most important thing. And on the most important thing, that's where you get to the advice that Eric Schmidt gave Sheryl Sandberg, which is like, "Hey, it's a rocket ship. Get on. Don't ask what seat I'm in. Just get on." (00:42:59): If it's the most important thing, you're going to get a smaller piece. Everyone wants to be there. Get the piece. If it's the most important thing, get the piece that you can crush, kill, do a great job at and grow from, because you're going to get a ton of visibility, you're going to get a ton of experience. You're going to see what it looks like in the fire, in the fire, and that is invaluable. You will use that everywhere. And so I say that. That's at project selection time, but now I'll be cautious. Understand, projects that start in the fire, hopefully, are forged in some manner of metal that cools and is no longer in the fire, like God willing. And likewise, things like dams that are holding up floodwaters have a tendency to crack or break or floods overcome [inaudible 00:43:42]. So I think you do want to be at selection time in one of those two places, but then you also... You're going to stick with the ride. (00:43:50): And again, to my point, if you're not engaged, if you aren't doing great work, if you don't love it, then move on. If you've exhausted it, you used to love it, but you don't anymore, move on. If you still love it and you're engaged, great. That's cool. That's a great thing. You deserve to go from the forge to the dam and back over time. You don't have to always just keep jumping onto the latest fire. I tried to do that once, after the ad [inaudible 00:44:14]. Actually, so I spent six months and we built the first mobile ad product in 2012 and kind of saved the IPO, which had gotten pretty grim [inaudible 00:44:23]-
turns.zh: 是的，听着（00:42:12），在平等的情况下，两个地方都很不错。一个是，在公司没关注但你认为很重要的领域大显身手。这需要付出大量努力。你得全力以赴，真正在那里攻克难关。因为我向你保证，作为高管，当有巨大的拦水坝阻挡洪水时，你会对那个顶住大坝的人敬佩不已。你会说：“继续加油，阿特拉斯，你做得很棒。”第二个最佳选择，或者说同样重要的选择，是专注于最重要的事情。在最重要的事情上，你会得到更小的份额。但每个人都想参与其中。抓住机会。只要是关键任务，就能获得大量关注和经验。你会见识到火场中的真实场景，而这份经验无比珍贵。日后你会处处受益。所以我这么说。这是在项目选择时要考虑的，但现在我要谨慎一些。要明白，刚开始在火场中拼搏的项目，最终往往会冷却下来，再也无法承受压力。同样，拦水坝如果出了问题，洪水就会决堤（00:43:42）。所以我认为，在项目选择时，你应该选择这两个中的一个，但之后你得坚持到底。（00:43:50）再说回我的观点，若你不投入工作、表现不佳、对工作失去热情，那就离开。如果你已经精疲力竭、曾经热爱但现在不再热爱，那就离开。但如果你依然热爱并全身心投入，那很棒。这很棒。你值得从火场到拦水坝，再回归的过程。你不必总是追逐最新热点。有一次，我试过这样做，在广告项目（00:44:14）之后。实际上，我花了六个月时间，在2012年开发了首款移动广告产品，成功挽救了当时已陷入困境的IPO（00:44:23）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I remember that.
turns.zh: 是的，我记得那件事。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: ... that point. And I told Mark, I was like, "This is so fun. Maybe you can just keep doing this, just putting me on the biggest fire every six months." And he turns to me, he said, "Buzz, that's not a real job." (00:44:32): He's like, "I need you to stay here and usher this forward," which I did for the next four and a half years. And it was amazing. It was amazing. And again, I do give him such... It's funny, I'm going to get a hard time in this. One of our biggest critics as well as being one of his biggest fans. I have both those jobs, but today we're talking about stuff that I think Mark really demonstrates really well. And he did a great job of pushing me in my career to different places where I didn't think I could succeed. And he saw the opportunity that made it happen.
turns.zh: ……那个观点。我当时对马克说：“这太有趣了。也许你可以每六个月就让我参与最紧急的项目。”他转过身对我说：“巴兹，这可不是真正的工作。” （00:44:32）他说：“我需要你留在这里推进这项工作。” 接下来的四年半，我一直这么做。这太棒了。太棒了。再说回来，确实要给他点赞。有趣的是，我可能会因此受到批评。毕竟他既是我们最严厉的批评者，也是最忠实的支持者。我两者都是，但今天我们要谈论马克真正出色的地方。他在推动我的职业生涯方面做得非常出色，带我去了很多我认为自己无法成功的地方。他看到了让我成功的机会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What have you learned about that, giving Mark negative criticism, anything that he accepts? What do you learned about that?
turns.zh: 关于这一点，你学到了什么？向马克提出负面批评，他能接受吗？你从中学到了什么？

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Mark's voracious for all information and all points of view. One of the things that's pretty interesting, I talked earlier about how much, as a founder, I think especially, you have to have tremendous conviction. You just have to have a tremendous degree of confidence. And I think Mark is somebody who is maybe the strongest willpower of a person I've ever met, just in a pure willpower sense. One thing that's interesting about Mark is you'll give him feedback, he listens. He's a kind person to work for, so you'll give him feedback, and he'll listen. Truly. He'll most often tell you that you're wrong, why you're wrong. That's just like most often. And what will happen is... It's uncanny. It's like over the course of the next week or two, you'll just see shifts. And I don't think he's doing it... (00:45:55): I've always joked that the information gets to him. So much information every day gets him. And then at night, he re-compiles the whole world with all that information and comes back. And by the way, this is not just true about product work. In my head, I was thinking about product stuff where he was like, "Hey, I think this product is doing this wrong." He's like, "No, no, that's why it's not that way." And the product will start to shift. Also to give him feedback just on his own presence in a meeting or delivery, he'll be like, "Oh, well here's why I did it that way." And then a couple weeks later, you'll get in a similar situation, and he will moderate how he shows up. So I actually find him somebody who's really satisfying to give him feedback. It really works. It's very effective, but you do have to take the long view on it. And he will have a... The things he did, he didn't do an accident. He will have a reason why he did them the way he did them.
turns.zh: 马克对所有信息和观点都如饥似渴。有一件很有趣的事，我之前说过，作为创始人，我认为你尤其需要拥有极强的信念。你必须具备极高的自信心。我认为马克的意志力可能是我见过最强大的人之一，单论意志力而言。他会听取你的反馈意见，非常善于接纳批评。他通常会告诉你你错了，并解释原因。这是他最常做的事。接下来，神奇的事情就会发生……在接下来的一两周内，你会看到明显的转变。我不认为他是刻意为之的。（00:45:55）我常开玩笑说信息会渗透到他的大脑。他每天接收海量信息，到了晚上，他会用这些信息重新构建整个世界。顺便说一句，这不仅适用于产品工作。在我看来，当我对产品提出改进建议时，他会说：“嘿，我觉得这个产品做得不对。”我反驳道：“不，不，这就是为什么它不该那样做。”然后产品就会开始调整方向。同样，当你就他在会议或演示中的表现给他反馈时，他也会说：“哦，嗯，这就是我那样做的原因。” 几周后，当你遇到类似情况时，他会调整自己的表现方式。所以我觉得给他反馈真的很有收获。这很有效，但你必须有长远的眼光。他所做的每一件事都不是偶然的。他总有自己的深层考量。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's a great example of strong opinions, loosely held.
turns.zh: 这就是所谓“持开放态度的坚定信念”的典范。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Yeah, that's right.
turns.zh: 是啊，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It also makes me think, I think you used the compiler analogy. I'm thinking the model training. He's retrained his model overnight.
turns.zh: 这也让我想到，你之前用了编译器的比喻。我在想模型训练。他一夜之间重新训练了模型。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Yeah, that's right. It's funny. One of the things that's so funny about Mark is if you give him some feedback in the morning, the next six meetings he has, whether it's about that product or not, he'll ask people what they think of that feedback. He won't attribute. He's just like, "Hey, what do you think about this in this product? And so you'll be in a meeting with him and you'll see him doing it. He'll come to the meeting with you about some other topic. He'll be like, "Hey boss, what do you think about this product and this idea?" And so he will, over the course of the day, take that little note and kind of pressure test it, and he loves to triangulate. Where are all the points of view on this that maybe you didn't see? So he really values a broad perspective on each thing that's being discussed, which is really fun.
turns.zh: 是啊，说得对。真有趣。马克最有趣的地方在于，如果你早上给他反馈，接下来六个会议，无论是否涉及那个产品，他都会问别人对反馈意见的看法。他不会归功于任何人，而是会说：“嘿，你们对这个产品有什么看法？” 所以他会在一天内反复验证那些小建议，喜欢三角验证。他会寻找所有可能被你忽视的观点。所以他真的很重视讨论中的广泛视角，这真的很有趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Trying to get more training data for his model. I get it.
turns.zh: 努力为他的模型获取更多训练数据。我懂了。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: You can't get me to call Mark an LLM. That's not fair. That's [inaudible 00:47:35].
turns.zh: 你们可别让我叫马克LLM。这不公平。这是[00:47:35听不清]。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We could all hope to be as smart as Mark. As you were talking, I noticed your tattoos, and it reminded me that you've got at least two tattoos that I'm aware of.
turns.zh: 我们都希望能像马克一样聪明。你说话的时候，我注意到你的纹身，这让我想起你至少有两个纹身，我知道的。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Oh, yeah.
turns.zh: 哦，是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One is of California, which I completely understand. California is a very special place, but you have this other tattoo that is just the words Veritas. Can you talk about what that's about and why that's important to you?
turns.zh: 其中一个纹身来自加州，这我完全能理解。加州是个非常特别的地方，但你还有另一个纹身，写着“Veritas”这个词。你能谈谈这背后的含义，以及它为何对你如此重要吗？

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: The funny thing about tattoos in general is I came out of high school, I was like... I don't know if there was an archetype for me, but I didn't drink until I was 21. I was a very rule-following person. I was like, "Why are you going to get a tattoo, affect your body? "Why would you dye your hair? Just let it be what it was." And some of this was I think I was somebody who was privileged and had a great deal of self-confidence in who I was and what I wanted to be, and that was fine. But in some ways I was also weirdly judgey about other people in a way that's kind of off- brain for me, certainly today it would be, but at the time, getting a tattoo is a big deal for me. I was like, "Oh, this is just the vehicle for my life and you can do whatever you want with it. And it's not like a... It's something that you possess, and if you feel like if you want to decorate it, you can decorate it. (00:48:47): And so getting a tattoo was a big deal to me actually, and I completely shifted my mindset of how I thought about my body and how I thought about people's body and their presence and their time, maybe to some degree, even an understanding of mortality. Like, "Hey, can't take it with you. It's all going to go..." When you're 18, you think you're going to live forever, and by the time you're 22, a grizzled 22-year-old veteran, you're like, "Ah, tattoo that bad boy up. It's all going down." And so yeah, that's why I got the Veritas tattoo, which is Latin for truth, which is... I will say it's a little cheesy, because it's also Harvard's motto. But I got it in a monotype font. This is the programmer's font here. (00:49:28): The other thing that's interesting to me about tattoos was it's also part of a generational shift. We grew up in a time when tattoos were really seen by adults as gangs or bikers or sailors or certain types. Now my understanding, I saw a stat recently that more people in my generation have tattoos than don't have tattoos. And so I think we also just culturally shifted positions in a way that... I find richness of self-expression wonderful. I really think it's great. And so I'm here for all of it.
turns.zh:
说到纹身这个事儿，有趣的是我高中毕业后，当时我觉得……我不知道自己是否被刻板化了，但直到21岁我才开始喝酒。我一直是个循规蹈矩的人。我会想：“为什么要纹身？会影响身体形象啊？”“为什么要染发？就让它保持原样好了。” 我觉得部分原因是我曾被宠坏了，对自己和未来充满自信，这没什么问题。但有时我又对别人评头论足，这在我现在看来挺奇怪的，但当时确实如此。对我来说，纹身是个大决定。我会说：“哦，这不过是人生旅程的载体，你想怎么装饰都可以。反正它属于你自己，如果你想装饰它，那就去装饰。” （00:48:47）所以纹身对我意义非凡，它彻底改变了我对身体、他人、时间、甚至死亡的看法。比如，“嘿，带不走啊。一切都会消逝……” 18岁时你觉得自己能永生，而22岁时——一个经验丰富的22岁老手——你会说：“去纹那个纹身吧，一切都会过去的。” 所以这就是我纹“Veritas”的原因，这个拉丁词汇代表真理。我得承认它有点俗气，因为哈佛的校训也是这个。但我用了单字体字体。这可是程序员专用的字体啊（00:49:28）。

关于纹身还有个有趣的现象：它也标志着时代的变迁。我们成长的那个年代，纹身在成年人眼中是帮派、摩托党、海员的象征。如今据我了解，我这一代纹身的人比不纹身的多得多。所以文化观念确实在变迁……我觉得自我表达的多样性很棒，非常赞同。所以我完全支持这种文化现象。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: My assumption from what you're describing is, this idea of truth is very important to the way you think and work.
turns.zh: 从你描述的情况来看，我觉得“真理”这个概念对你思考和工作方式非常重要。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: My reputation does precede me on this point, I'm afraid, which is... I think when I was young, I saw being honest... And I was wrong by the way. I saw being honest as kind of a get out of jail free card. You could say whatever you wanted as long as you're being honest. That's just not the case at all. I've written about this before, but by far my biggest professional regrets were me not being kind. And I used to think... I wrote this note a while back called Be Kind, where being nice, that's like patronizing, or telling somebody things that are half-truths or just getting by. And I'm against that. But being kind isn't that. Being kind is like, "Hey, how can I deliver this feedback in a way that is actually productive and helpful, in a way that is going to help them and not cause them just to feel bad and helpless? (00:50:50): And I think I did that wrong a lot as a kid, as a young man. And so being honest is still a big part of my personality. No one would ever accuse me of being dishonest who knows me. And I think people understand and respect that I'm pretty direct, and if I have concerns or issues, I'm going to bring them up. I'm just much better at bringing them up now and expressing a true care and belief. I wouldn't bring it up if I didn't think we could do better, if I didn't think we could fix it, if I didn't believe in this situation. And so being honest is still a huge part of my identity, and I think that's something I'm very proud of. But I will say the contextualization of how I'm honest has changed immensely since I got this tattoo.
turns.zh: 恐怕在这件事上，我的名声在外。说起来……我年轻时曾把诚实视为某种"免罪金牌"——只要你说实话，就可以畅所欲言。事实远非如此。我曾写过相关文章，但至今为止，我最大的职业遗憾就是不够善良。过去我总以为……我曾写过一篇名为《善良至上》的文章，认为善良就是居高临下地教训别人，或者说些半真半假的话蒙混过关。我反对这种做法。但真正的善良不该是这样。善良应该是："嘿，我该如何以一种富有成效、真正有益的方式提供反馈，让对方受益而非感到挫败和无助？"（00:50:50）我年轻时在这方面做得很糟糕。所以，诚实至今仍是我性格中重要的一部分。认识我的人都不会说我不诚实。他们理解并尊重我的直率，如果我有顾虑或问题，就会提出来。如今我更擅长以真诚关怀和信念的方式提出问题。如果我不认为我们能做得更好、不能解决问题、对现状不抱信心，就绝不会提起。所以，诚实仍是我身份中重要的一部分，我为此深感自豪。但自从纹了这个纹身后，我对诚实的理解有了巨大转变。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That seems reasonable. This touches a little bit on something I definitely wanted to talk about, which is one of your most classic pieces, and this is the way I first learned about you, is a piece that is called Communication is the Job.
turns.zh: 这说得在理。这让我想起你最经典的作品之一，也是我最初了解你的途径——那篇名为《沟通是工作》的文章。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know many people have read this, many people haven't. I'd love for you to just talk about what this means and why this is important, why this is something that you wanted to share.
turns.zh: 我知道很多人读过这篇文章，也有很多没读过。我希望你能谈谈它的意义、它的重要性，以及你为何要分享这些观点。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Yeah, it's one of the things that, especially if you aspire to be a leader... And leadership isn't management, and leadership isn't being the only person responsible, it's not even always the same as accountability. But if you want to have an impact...
turns.zh: 是的，这正是如果你渴望成为领导者……领导力不等于管理，也不意味着独自承担责任，甚至不总是等同于问责。但如果你想产生影响……

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: It's not even always the same as accountability, but if you want to have an impact on the world around you, it is exclusively done through the creation of artifacts or verbalizations that affect other humans. That is all there is. That's all there is if you want to have an impact, if you want to create some kind of a lasting change. And it could be in your little relationship, it could be in your team, it could be in your company, it could be in the world. It is down to communication. And so often you hear people saying, "Oh yeah, I wrote that up a year ago." It's like, "Yeah, but you did a bad job of writing it up a year ago, or we would've not wasted a year not doing it." (00:52:47): People always think that's, "Oh, I had that idea," and that's means anything. It means nothing. It means absolutely nothing. Or it's like, "Oh, I wrote this post." Well, you didn't break through with it. That's on you. It's not on the audience. People want to blame the audience. Well, the audience is just there. I mentioned this even earlier, and I hope people caught it, when I said, "Hey," I give somebody a piece of work and they come back six months later and they have done the wrong thing, I'll take the L. I will take the L on it. It's not great for them. They'll be pissed they wasted their time, but like I said, that's my responsibility. I did not communicate clearly what I wanted, what the expectations were. (00:53:25): Could they have also helped themselves? Sure, they could have, and that's a thing that takes all sides. We should work on this problem for both angles. I have another post called Listening is the Job, which is the other side of this. But communication is the job is, I really believe... Actually, it's the relationship to this idea that came out of the US Marines and the SEALs of extreme ownership, which is... So whenever thing goes wrong, I ask myself, "What could I have done differently in terms of how I communicated things for this to have gone better?" Could I have set priorities better? Could I have set expectations better? Did I need to have a better metric that I pointed the team at? Did I put the wrong people on it? (00:54:04): By the way, the thing I talk about is org charts are communication devices. They don't exist. There's not a physical string between you and your manager. They're just communication tools that are supposed to give people a rough sense of how things are organized and where to go with who. And so all these things are communication. Silence is communication, me not reaching out to you to check on you, to check on your project. We talked about the [inaudible 00:54:29] earlier. What does that mean? That means trust. That means responsibility. The absence of check-ins has meaning. You cannot not communicate. You are always communicating something with your face, with your clothes, with your body. What are you communicating? (00:54:45): I'll give you a funny example, which I hope we get to put in the podcast, because if you're watching this on video, you will have noticed that my camera cannot stop adjusting light. It's just constantly too dark or too bright. I'm trying a new camera. I'm a nerdy guy. I try a lot of camera gear, I try a lot of microphone gear. I love to have all the latest gadgets and gizmos, so I'm trying something new. It's not working. And in my head I'm like, what is this communicating about me? People are going to think that I don't care or that I'm not competent. (00:55:15): That's what I'm talking about. And now, I felt compelled to explain it in the podcast so that I can communicate clearly that that's not the case. I really just think so much of what I try to do in my professional life is understand the mental model of other people. Where are they right now? And I mean specific people, like my managers or my key technical leaders, and I mean general people like teams, and I mean broadly just the average human. Where are they at in this conversation? And how can I craft my language, my presence, my persona, everything to usher them from where they are to where I want to get them? (00:55:52): And that requires me to have a very clear idea of where I want to get them, have to have a clear idea of where they are. And I want to tell you, it's not as much work as it sounds like. I think no one would accuse me of having this big fabricated persona. It's not that. But it is having tremendous empathy for where people are starting. That was the lead for me. All the rest of it, all the rest of how I show up in meetings trying to smile more, because I'm like a big scary guy, those things are little things that you work on and they become second nature and they're easy. The hard thing is just having the empathy for your audience and being, "Where are they? Where are they starting?" And when you miss taking responsibility for that, extreme responsibility for that.
turns.zh:
问责制甚至不总是与此同义，但如果你想对周遭世界产生影响，就必须通过创作出能影响他人的成果或言论来实现。这就是全部真相。如果你想产生持久的改变，无论是在亲密关系中、团队里、公司里，还是在整个世界里——关键在于沟通。  

你常听到人们说：“哦，是啊，我一年前写了那个报告。”但这根本无济于事！问题在于你当时写得太糟糕了，否则我们就不会浪费一整年时间来纠错。人们总爱把责任推给听众，但听众只是被动接受者。  

我之前提到过，当我把一份工作交给别人，六个月后他们做错了事，我会主动承担责任。这对他们来说很糟糕，他们会为浪费时间而生气，但这责任在我。我没有清晰传达期望，没有明确要求。  

他们本可以自我改进吗？当然可以，但这需要双方共同努力。我还有一篇文章叫《倾听才是职责》，从另一个角度探讨这个问题。但我坚信，沟通才是关键……这源自美国海军陆战队和海豹突击队的“极端所有权”理念。每当事情出错时，我都会反思：“在沟通方面，我本可以做得更好吗？我本可以更明确优先级吗？设定更清晰的期望吗？为团队提供更有效的衡量标准吗？还是选错了团队成员？” 

顺便说一句，我认为组织结构图就是沟通工具。它们并非实体存在。没有你和上司之间连接的物理线条。它们只是沟通工具，旨在让人们大致了解组织架构和工作分配。  

沉默也是一种沟通方式。比如我不主动联系你询问进展，不检查你的项目进度。我们之前讨论过的“[听不清00:54:29]”现象，这意味着什么？这意味着信任和责任。缺乏跟进本身就传递了信息。你无法做到不沟通。你的面容、穿着、肢体语言都在传递信息。  

举个有趣的例子——希望能在播客中提到这个——如果你看视频版，应该注意到我的摄像头总在调整光线。要么太暗，要么太亮。我在测试新相机。我是个技术控，经常尝试各种摄影设备和麦克风，喜欢拥有最新玩意儿，但这次新相机效果不佳。在我脑海里，我在想，这相机在传递什么信息？人们会觉得我不在乎或者不专业。  

这就是我要强调的重点。现在，我觉得有必要在播客中详细解释，让大家更清楚沟通的真谛。
显然事实并非如此。我真的认为，我在职业生涯中所做的大部分工作，就是去理解他人的思维模式。他们现在处于什么阶段？这里指的具体人物，比如我的经理或关键技术领导者；也指更广泛的群体，比如团队，以及普通大众。我需要清楚他们在对话中的位置，然后调整我的语言、举止和个人形象，引导他们从现有状态走向我期望的目标。（00:55:52）这就要求我必须先明确自己的目标，再准确把握他们的现状。我想告诉大家，这项工作远比听起来容易得多。没人会指责我刻意伪装自己。我所强调的，是真诚理解他人的出发点。这才是关键所在。其余的细节，比如在会议中多微笑示人（毕竟我看上去是个严肃的人），这些都是可以通过刻意练习养成的习惯，久而久之自然而然。真正困难的是，要保持对听众的同理心，时刻问自己："他们现在在哪里？他们从哪里出发的？"而当你忽视对此承担起责任时，那就是严重的失职了。
