turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: I'll give you a couple. One is multimodality. There's an old saying, repetition never spoiled the prayer. And I think most experienced communicators, whether they be writers, whether they be public speakers, talk about the importance of reiterating a point several times and in several different ways to make sure that people have a chance to internalize it. You want to use it, you want to say it directly, you want to use metaphor. And so for me, I will give an all-hands and then write a post with the content of the all-hands, because different people are going to respond differently to these modalities and are going to absorb information at different rates on these different modalities. That's a trivial one. (00:57:23): Another one that I think of all the time is making sure that you address people's fears and concerns. People will not listen to you if they think you don't know what's going on. And so, one of my favorite things to do when we're talking about some kind of issue is right up top and say, "Hey, let me be clear. This is the issue we're having. I know we're having it. I know what matters." And then I'll say the same thing that I would've said, but they would've literally ignored me, because how can they trust my conclusions if they don't accept the premise? You know what I'm saying? I think there's a whole piece there. Obviously when you're in person, it's a lot easier because you're reading facial expressions. Even on this, I'm reading you nodding on that. I'm like, "Okay, he's with me." And then I throw in a, "You know what I mean?" Whereas if you give me a cocked head, I then bring a second example to try to drive the point home. But you build yourself up. Most people are going to realistically start in their careers trying to influence one or two people. That's where you start. One or two people. That's who you got to communicate with. Your manager, one teammate, that's who you got. And then you build up and build up and build up a skillset to do it at a larger and larger scale.
turns.zh: 我举几个例子。第一个是多模态交流。有一句老话叫“重复祈祷永不败”。我觉得大多数有经验的沟通者，无论是作家还是公众演说家，都强调要用多种方式多次重复一个观点，这样才能让人们有机会真正理解。既要用文字表达，又要用口语传达，还要用比喻。所以对我来说，开完全体会议后，我会写一篇帖子，把会议内容总结出来，因为不同的人对这些沟通方式的反应不同，吸收信息的速度也各不相同。这很简单。（00:57:23）：另一个我常想的点是，要确保消除人们的恐惧和担忧。如果人们觉得你不了解情况，就不会听你说话。所以当我们讨论某个问题时，首先要明确说：“嘿，我说清楚了，这是我们面临的问题。我知道问题所在。”然后我会重复一遍自己原本要说的话，但他们可能根本不听，因为如果他们不接受前提条件，又怎么会信任你的结论呢？懂我的意思吧？我觉得这里面有很多东西。显然面对面交流更容易，因为你能读懂对方的面部表情。就连现在，我都能看到你点头表示同意。我就知道你理解了。然后我会说一句“懂我的意思吧？”而如果你摇头，我就会举第二个例子，试图让他们明白。但你要逐步积累。大多数人在职业生涯初期都会试图影响一两个人。这就是起点。一两个人。这就是你要沟通的对象。你的经理、一个队友，就是这些人。然后你不断积累技能，逐步扩大影响范围。

turns.en: Actually, Mark and I tried it together and I want to say, first of all, when the headset came out, we breathed a little sigh of relief because the stuff inside of it didn't represent a fundamental breakthrough. Everything inside of it was something that we probably could have gone and done, with the exception of Apple silicon, which is a marvel, but it's worth nothing. Apple Silicon is like a 2X marvel when doing things like scaling display resolution is unfortunately a quadratic proposition, and so a 2X linear scaling advantage doesn't buy you as much as you might expect when you're trying to scale resolution. And so that was step one. But we still assumed at that price point, with their legendary attention to detail and polish, they probably produced a great product. If you want an outstanding, best possible headset for the money, we've got it. It's the Quest 3." (01:01:55): And I was so thrilled when I tried the AVP next to Mark, we were like, "No, we think we have the actual best headset." Now, we're not saying it's the best at all things. If you're sitting still and watching a movie a high-res movie, Apple Vision Pro is really great. It's really great. The resolution shines. The way they've tuned the pass-through shines if you're stationary and looking straight ahead. And they've done some really nice things with the UI. It's one of these things that we do get annoyed about, a mile aside, we get a little bit annoyed about as product people. (01:02:31): I know that this happens to all of us. It happens to Apple, happens to Google, happens to us. We have a bunch of internal things we've been playing with, which will at some point ship and we will be accused of having stolen them when we actually did not steal them. If you want, you can go see my Quora answer on the history of the like button where this happened previously, where we had built the like button internally before it was launched elsewhere. Anyways, it's a whole thing. This happens in our industry a lot, and I really shouldn't care as much. It's a little bit of my ego peeking through, which I should control and tamp down, if I'm being responsible. (01:03:03): The beautiful UI polishes, they did a tremendous job with eye tracking. One of the things that's interesting about the eye tracking is, to do it the way they've done it, that's why you have to have the prescription insert, so it doesn't support your glasses. You have to get prescription inserts. They're expensive. And they can shoot the cameras that track your eyes through the lens as well as the light around it. Ours go from the side on the Quest Pro, and that allows you to wear corrective lenses. (01:03:27): And so different choices like that have trade-offs, but it's still cool. And some people are characterizing it incorrectly on the internet. They're doing a characterization up close to the lens. Once you factor in the eye relief, the distance between where the lenses are and your eyeball is, their field of view gets pretty narrow for almost all faces relative to ours, which I find distracting. (01:03:59): Their displays are much dimmer than ours, and I find the motion blur really distracting when I'm in mixed reality use cases. (01:05:05): But people don't even know that the Quest 3, you can do Remote Desktop. They truly have. I think it's tremendous. I certainly celebrate a large number of Apple product. I'm a huge fan of their work. I'm a huge fan of what they do. That's probably why I expected more from the AVP.
turns.zh:
实际上，我和马克一起试用了这款产品。首先我想说，当耳机上市时，我们松了一口气，因为它的内部技术并没有实现根本性的突破。除了苹果自研芯片（这确实是个奇迹，但对提升显示分辨率这种复杂需求作用有限），其他配置我们完全可以自己研发。这是第一步。但我们当时假设，凭借苹果传奇般的注重细节和精良工艺，他们的产品应该会非常出色。一周前我在和马修·鲍尔的播客中说了这番话："听着，我们本准备上市时宣称这是性价比最高的耳机。若你想用最划算的钱买到最出色的产品，我们推荐Quest 3。" （01:01:55）当我和马克一起试用AVP耳机时，我们惊喜地发现："不，我们认为Quest 3才是真正最好的耳机。" 当然，我们并非认为它在所有方面都无可匹敌。比如看高清电影时，Apple Vision Pro的表现确实惊艳——分辨率出色，直视前方时的通透效果堪称典范，UI设计也精良。但作为产品从业者，我们对某些细节难免有些不满（尽管这只是次要问题）。（01:02:31）这种情况在我们行业屡见不鲜。苹果、谷歌都曾遇到过类似问题。我们内部也有许多创新成果，最终被指控抄袭。虽然我们确实从未窃取他人技术，但这种指控仍会困扰我们。想了解更多背景，可以看看我在Quora上的回答，讲解点赞按钮的历史——我们内部开发的点赞按钮在别处发布前就被抄袭了。总之，这种争执在行业中屡见不鲜，我本不该太在意，但有时会被自己的虚荣心左右。（01:03:03）苹果的UI设计精美，眼动追踪技术也堪称典范。但要注意，眼动追踪的实现需要配戴专用镜片，这意味着无法与普通眼镜兼容。（01:03:27）手部追踪功能更胜一筹。应用生态方面，显然苹果的表现更优，但这对他们不算公平——毕竟刚上市且销量有限。但舒适度最令我失望——Apple Vision Pro的视场角过小。网上有些误解，将评测标准局限于镜头附近的区域。若考虑到眼间距（即镜头与眼球的距离），相对我们的产品，其视场角几乎所有用户都偏窄，这让我深感遗憾。
让人分心的。（01:03:59）：他们的显示屏比我们的暗很多，而且当我在混合现实场景中使用时，画面模糊真的很让人分心。正如我之前在播客中提到的，我是一个混合现实的狂热爱好者。正是因为同样的原因，我也非常看好它的潜力——顺便说一句，我认为手势交互和混合现实让更多人能更轻松地体验到它。我很高兴我们套装里有控制器，因为它极大地扩展了可操作性。我们使用电脑时不止用一种设备，我们有键盘、鼠标，一直在使用多种交互方式。我真的觉得我们传输模式的舒适度、缺乏视野模糊和画面抖动，以及显示屏的亮度，让我感叹：“天哪，如果让我选一个，我会选Quest 3。”（01:04:40）：现在有人说得没错：“这太偏颇了。” 当然偏颇。去形成自己的看法吧。但最让我气愤的是，大多数人根本没试过Quest 3。这才是最让我无语的。如果你去试试Quest 3，问问自己，你是愿意拥有七台Quest 3（自己一台，六台给好朋友），还是一台Apple Vision Pro？我相信对每个人来说，答案都不是Quest 3。有些人确实有非常适合他们生活的使用场景，那就选择Apple Vision Pro，我完全没意见。（01:05:05）：但人们甚至不知道Quest 3支持远程桌面功能。你可以通过非常流行的 Remote Desktop 应用来实现，或者在工作室中用三台显示器环绕，实时传输电脑画面。我觉得很多用户就是没下功夫。他们甚至没试过。我欢迎那些认为我偏颇的人去验证，但别光说不练，真去试试 Quest 3 再下结论，因为这确实是一款很棒的设备。多花3000美元能解锁更多可能性。（01:05:38）：顺便说一句，他们怎么能这么做呢？我们推出售价1299美元的头显时，人们都疯狂了。他们会说：“啊，3500美元？没关系。这无所谓。谁在乎呢？” 我不知道。公平太难奢求了，反正我不在乎。苹果建立了如此强大的品牌，这确实了不起。我当然很欣赏许多苹果产品。我是他们工作的忠实粉丝。这大概就是我对AVP期望过高的原因吧。

turns.en: Well, I'll show you my favorite AR device, which is these Ray-Bans. I actually bought them.
turns.zh: 嗯，我来给你们展示一下我最喜欢的增强现实设备——这副雷朋眼镜。实际上，我自己买了它们。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Here, I'll put them on it. Here, what I'm going to do is I'm going to record. I didn't tell you I was going to do this. I'm going to record this as we're talking. Look at this.
turns.zh: 来，我戴上给你看看。现在我要做的是边聊天边录视频。看看这个。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: I like that. They look so good on you too. This is a good fit.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个款式。戴在你脸上也很合适。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: My mother-in-law's like, "You look so sophisticated. You look really smart with these on." And we bought these actually to film our kids, or our kid, instead of having Cameron's face. And it's been awesome.
turns.zh: 我岳母说：“你看起来太成熟了。戴上这个眼镜，你看起来特别聪明。”我们买这副眼镜的初衷是想给孩子们拍视频，而不是让镜头对着卡梅伦的脸。结果效果棒极了。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: It's really the best. It is so hard to look at a phone screen and have the real thing be in between you. No, the glass is the way to do it.
turns.zh: 这玩意儿真是太棒了。看手机屏幕和真实场景比起来，差别太大了。不，还是用玻璃屏幕更靠谱。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Look at this, my new look. I'm just going to have glasses on all the time.
turns.zh: 看看我的新造型吧。我以后都要戴着眼镜了。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: We got to get you the multimodal. I've been playing with that since December, where you can use the camera to ask a Meta AI assistant about things. It's really good. I was in a ski village recently with my family and I had them on. I'm just like, "Hey, take a look. Tell what you see." And I had found a sign and it gave me directions. "Hey, the bathrooms are down those stairs to the right. Do you want food? It's over to the right." It couldn't tell what village I was in, but it was like, "You're in a ski village somewhere. Here's the amenities." And I was like, "Wow." There's something real magical here.
turns.zh: 我们得给你弄一副多模态设备。我从去年12月就开始玩了，可以用摄像头向Meta AI助手提问。效果特别棒。最近我和家人在一个滑雪村，用它拍照。我说：“嘿，看看这儿有什么。告诉我你看到什么。”我找到一个指示牌，它给我指了方向。“卫生间在右边的楼梯下去。想吃东西吗？在右边。”虽然它没识别出我在哪个滑雪村，但还是提示：“你现在在某个滑雪村。附近有便利设施。”我惊叹道：“哇。”这技术真是太神奇了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like I need this for my podcasting interview so I could just have a little voice tell me questions to be asking and where I'm at.
turns.zh: 我觉得这对我的播客采访会很有帮助，这样就能有个小声音告诉我该问什么问题，或者提示我现在在哪儿。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Right, totally. Yeah.
turns.zh: 对啊，完全正确。是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How helpful would that be?
turns.zh: 那会有多实用呢？

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Okay, I'm going to cheat on this one and say, obviously we've been talking for a while, but playing with glasses that have full AR capabilities, and we've got one that has rumored to be coming internally soon, so heavily rumored in fact that you might even say it's almost been confirmed. And what's been really fun is being able to play with these time machines, really, in terms of what they are. It's amazing technology. People were giving us speeches, big company-wide speeches, and had all their notes on the glasses. And they could control the slides just using a gesture.
turns.zh: 好吧，我这次就偷个懒，直接说吧。显然我们已经聊了很久，但玩玩这些具备全AR功能的眼镜，特别是据传即将内部推出的那款，传闻如此之多，甚至可以说几乎已经确定了。最有趣的是能玩这些“时间机器”，准确来说就是它们的本质。技术太惊人了。有人给我们做演讲，公司级的演讲，所有笔记都显示在眼镜上。你甚至可以用手势控制幻灯片。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh my God.
turns.zh: 天哪。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: There's exciting things afoot. The future's looking pretty bright.
turns.zh: 未来真是充满惊喜。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something that I wanted to touch on, which is when Mark put out this whole video of, "Here's what I think of Apple Vision Pro versus the Quest," a lot of people are just like, "Oh man, because he's putting out this video, he must be so afraid of what's happening and it's not the right move." What went into thinking? Was there strategic thinking there? Was it just him, "Here's what I think?"
turns.zh: 还有个我想提一下的，马克发布了整个视频，比较Apple Vision Pro和Quest。很多人就说：“哦天哪，他发布这个视频，肯定是对现状很恐慌，这不是明智之举。”他是出于什么考虑呢？是经过战略考量吗？还是他就想说：“这是我的看法？”

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: This guy does [inaudible 01:08:30] about the modern era. Everyone's in their Meta head about everything. Everything's a four-dimensional chess. That was just what Mark thought of the thing. That's what he thought about it. I think he wanted to make sure people remembered, hey, Quest 3 is literally a better device, and people haven't even tried it. (01:08:46): And so we're not always playing four-dimensional chess over here. Sometimes we're just like, "Here's a thing that I believe is true. I'm going to say it out loud with my mouth." That's what he did. It's not that hard. When I do it, everyone expects it because of my persona or brand or whatever the thing is. I guess people are surprised when a CEO does it. All right, I get that. That's cool. There's other sets of societal expectations there. (01:09:08): And we're all familiar with Apple putting the Welcome IBM ad in the New York Times, and then Slack doing the same thing with Microsoft and the Ballmer iPhone comments. None of those were true discussions of the technical merits of a product. Those were all just big, rally the troops gestures. This is not that. Mark is deep. He's an expert in this stuff. I'm an expert in this stuff. I feel great about our choices. (01:09:39): By the way, when I've used it, I could get myself completely into the head of the person who designed it. I can tell you from using it what instructions they were given, that team was given. I can tell you what they were optimizing for. I can tell you what constraints they were under. By all the choices they made, I can tell you all those things and I understand it coheres in that way. We made different choices. It shouldn't surprise anyone. We like our choices better. We could have made those choices. We didn't make those choices. We made these other choices. (01:10:06): And so for me, the weight, the wire, which just always brushes against my ear, the pocketable thing, I get it. That's not what I would've done, and I know that because I had the chance to do it and I chose not to. I don't know. I don't know why people are surprised. This wasn't some big, savvy strategic move. This was just, Mark's got a chance to use it. He's like, "Oh man, I think we should tell people what the real story is here." And we did.
turns.zh: 这家伙对现代社会真是有一套看法。每个人都沉浸在元宇宙的狂热之中，动不动就把一切上升到四维象棋的层面。那只是马克对此事的看法。他觉得有必要让人们记住：嘿，Quest 3确实是一款更出色的设备，可人们甚至还没试过呢。（01:08:46）：所以我们在这里可不是总在玩四维象棋。有时我们只是想说：“这是我坚信的事实，我要大声说出来。”他就是这么做的。这没那么难。当我这么做时，大家会因为我的个人形象或品牌效应而习以为常。但当一位CEO这么做时，人们可能就会感到惊讶。好吧，我理解。这很酷。社会对不同角色的期望确实不同。（01:09:08）：我们都熟悉苹果在《纽约时报》刊登“欢迎IBM”的广告，以及Slack针对微软和鲍尔默的iPhone评论事件。这些都不是对产品技术优点的真正探讨，只是激发团队士气的象征性举动。本次事件并非如此。马克深有见地。他是这方面的专家。我也是。我对我们的选择深感满意。（01:09:39）：顺便说一句，我用过后，能完全理解设计者的思路。我能根据使用体验判断他们接收了怎样的设计指令，团队面临怎样的优化目标，承受着哪些限制。通过他们的每个决策，我能拼凑出完整的逻辑链。我们做了不同的选择。这没什么好惊讶的。我们更偏爱自己的选择。我们本可以做出那些选择，但我们没有选择。我们选择了其他方案。（01:10:06）：对我来说，耳挂式设计、可收纳设计、轻便设计，这些我都懂。但那不是我会做的选择。我知道这一点，因为我有机会尝试却选择了放弃。我不知道为什么人们会惊讶。这不是什么高明的战略决策。马克只是抓住了机会，他说：“天哪，我觉得我们应该告诉人们真相。”然后我们就这么做了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that insight. And I know a lot of people watching are like, "Oh, shit, he's right. Wow. I didn't think of it that way." And so I think it had a lot of that impact. (01:10:41): I want to zoom out a little bit and talk about Meta's journey over the past couple years. It feels like there is a huge downturn in public perception of Meta and the stock price, and then over the past couple of years there's been a huge turnaround. And it feels like there's always a lot to learn from these periods. Just as an example of the stock price, I was just looking at it, it was down to $80-ish, and now today it's $487.
turns.zh: 我很欣赏这种见解。我知道很多观众会想：“哦，该死，他说得太对了。哇，我从没这么想过。”所以我觉得这段话产生了很大的影响。（01:10:41）：我想把视野放宽一点，谈谈Meta过去几年的历程。公众对Meta的看法和股价都经历了剧烈波动，但过去几年间情况发生了巨大转变。从这些波动中总能汲取不少经验。就股价而言，我刚看了一下，之前最低跌到80美元左右，而现在已经涨到了487美元。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm curious just what you've learned from going through that downturn and turnaround. And I know it's still in progress, but just what have you learned from that journey?
turns.zh: 我很好奇，你从经历的低谷和反弹中吸取了哪些教训。我知道这过程还在继续，但你从这段历程中学到了什么？

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Yeah. Well, there's a lot to take away, I got to tell you. I think we had the largest single day stock drop in history, followed 18 months later by this largest single day gain in stock market history.
turns.zh: 是啊，我得说能总结出很多经验。我们经历了史上最大单日股价暴跌，18个月后又创下股市史上最大单日涨幅。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh my God.
turns.zh: 天哪。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: As the legendary Lou Holtz said, " You're never as good as they say you are when you're winning, and you're never as bad as they say you are when you're losing." Mark has always brought that quote out to guide us internally to try to insulate ourselves a little bit from the vagaries of external opinion. And that's not just true with stock prices. That's true with media and press. It's true across a lot of things. (01:11:53): One of the things I told my team, and I still have to repeat it to them, is, "One of the things that's hard to remember when you're in it is that you know more than the critics do. You know more than the analysts in the marketplace do. You know more than the media does. You know more than the podcasters do. You know more than the Twitter does. You know more about what's real and substantial of value about our company than they do. That doesn't mean ignore them, because they have a different perspective and you need to understand it. Even if the totality is less than what you know, it may contain parts that you do not know." I'm a huge fan, I read the criticism of everything, and I read it very carefully, looking out for confirmation bias, looking out for things that I might be inclined to resist but are maybe true. I invite all critique, but I also don't accept the critique blindly. I don't just say, "Yes, this is obviously true." (01:12:55): Gell-Mann Amnesia is a great concept for everyone to understand. Gell-Mann Amnesia is this property where you'll read a newspaper article, let's say newspaper, why not, about a thing about which you are an expert, and you'll be baffled because here is an article that is not just wrong, it's inverted causality. Michael Crichton, I'll steal Michael Crichton's quote on this, "It's a wet sidewalks make rain story." And you'll be like, "What a terrible, bizarre story." (01:13:22): And then you will turn the page of the newspaper and it will be another article about a topic about which you know nothing, and you will read it as if it is the gospel truth. You'll figure it's, "Oh, no, look at this information about this foreign situation." Like I said, perfectly true. We should be smarter than that. And so does that mean you don't read the thing? No, you read it. You just read everything with that perspective of, "Wait a second, this is another point of view. And how do I integrate that into a whole perspective that I can have and be informed about?" (01:13:55): The first, the macro thing is taking the long view, realizing that when you're in the dumps, it's not as bad as you think, when you're at the top, it's not as good as you think. It's somewhere in between at all times. The second thing is communication is the job. We really did not communicate effectively, I think, with the market around our future investments. And listen, we've had two 10-year long huge investment areas. One has been AI, one has been reality labs. And AI's looking pretty good today. I can't think we can all agree with Lama 2, with Fair, the breakthroughs that we've had. (01:14:33): People don't notice that Fair, our AI research lab, is the second most cited research lab in AI behind Google. We've been doing this work. We didn't come here casually. We've been doing it, and so that's looking pretty good. I don't think we did enough to explain those best to people. Previously, the core business was going strong enough and they were willing to ignore them. And with the old Warren Buffett quote, "It's only when the tide goes out, we see who's not wearing swimming trunks." And so when the tide went out, when you have the Ukraine war and an interest rate hike and recessions, now everyone's scrambling for that incremental dollar and they're like, "Go get rid of this stuff." (01:15:15): And we had to tell the company, "You don't want to work at a company that, when times are tough, kills all future growth and just shores up in the core business." That's a company that's just committing itself to dying at some point, a little later than expected, but dying at some point. You want to work at a company that has a balanced portfolio of investments, which we had. We didn't explain that well, and so we spent that time explaining that to the market, to the press, to everybody. (01:15:38): And now, I think as people understand the size of it and the scope of it, and of course it helps that the core business has overcome its challenges there from ATT and the other kinds of stuff, it's looking pretty good. I do think one part is, as an internal person, really moderating your attachment to the external narratives and swings, that's super important. And you do that based on understanding your own expertise. And the second part is understanding why is there a delta. What is there? And grab that. It's usually communication.
turns.zh:
正如传奇人物卢·霍尔茨所说：“当你赢球时，人们总说你比实际更出色；当你输球时，人们又说你比实际更糟糕。” 马克经常引用这句话，提醒我们要保持客观，别被外界声音左右。这种情况不止适用于股价，也适用于媒体和舆论——几乎所有领域都存在类似的偏见。

（01:11:53）我曾告诉团队一句话，现在还要反复强调：“身处其中时，人们往往会忘记自己比批评者更懂行。我们比市场分析师更了解公司，比播客主更清楚现状，比推特用户更明白真相。这并不意味着要无视外界意见，而是要警惕确认偏差，审视那些可能被我们忽视的合理观点。即便整体观点与你的认知不符，仍可能蕴含着有价值的真知灼见。”

（01:12:55）盖尔-曼失忆症（Gell-Mann Amnesia）是每个人都应该理解的概念。面对专业领域的报道，人们会感到困惑，因为文章不仅逻辑混乱，甚至因果关系颠倒。引用迈克尔·克莱顿的话：“这就像‘湿滑的人行道导致下雨’的谬论。” 面对此类荒谬论点，人们会惊呼：“这简直是胡说八道！” 

（01:13:22）翻页到另一篇完全陌生领域的文章时，人们又会奉为真理。比如研究海外局势的报告。关键在于保持客观视角，审视不同观点：“等一下，换个角度看问题。”

（01:13:55）宏观层面要保持长远视野：低谷时别悲观，巅峰时别自满，状态总在波动之间。沟通是关键。我们在未来投资策略上未能有效传达信息。人工智能和现实实验室这两个十年级别的投资领域，前者如今成果斐然，后者突破性进展有目共睹。

（01:14:33）鲜为人知的是，专注人工智能的Fair实验室已成为AI领域引用次数第二多的研究机构。我们深耕不辍，绝非临时起意。沃伦·巴菲特曾说：“退潮时才看清谁没穿泳裤。” 当泡沫破裂时，真相才会浮出水面。
乌克兰战争、加息和经济衰退接踵而至，如今每个人都在拼命争夺每一笔可用资金，人们纷纷抛售资产，仿佛在说：“赶紧把这些东西处理掉吧。”（01:15:15）我们不得不告诫公司：“当经济形势艰难时，一味压缩未来增长空间、只专注于核心业务的公司注定要走向衰落。” 这样的公司注定会走向消亡，或许只是晚些时候才会倒闭。相反，我们希望员工能在一个投资组合均衡的公司工作，而这正是我们公司所具备的。但我们此前未能有效传达这一理念，因此我们花了大量时间向市场、媒体和公众解释这一点（01:15:38）。

如今，随着人们逐渐意识到公司业务的规模和广度（当然，核心业务克服了来自AT&T等方面的挑战也起到了助力作用），形势已然明朗。我认为，作为内部员工，关键在于要克制自己对外部市场叙事和波动的过度关注，这一点至关重要。这种克制源于对自身专业领域的深刻理解。另一方面，需要深入思考业务变动背后的深层原因，抓住关键要素——而这通常始于有效的沟通。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's also a big flattening of the org. This was something a lot of people talked about, where managers became ICs. Is there anything more there that you've learned of just how to adjust the org to be more efficient?
turns.zh: 组织架构也发生了重大扁平化。这是很多人讨论的话题，管理者逐渐转变为独立贡献者（IC）。对于如何调整组织架构以提高效率，你是否有更多见解？

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Of course, and I should have included that in the first section. I was a bit eager to wrap it up elegantly in the two. But you're right.
turns.zh: 当然，我本该在第一部分就提到这一点。我当时急于在两部分内容中做到简洁明了。不过你说得对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I appreciate it.
turns.zh: 非常感谢。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: We made significant shifts in how we operated the business, which was super painful. And listen, this goes back to the boom times of COVID, when it looked like there was a real lasting secular shift in things like e-commerce and in working remotely and these tool sits, which are exactly what we build, and it's primed us. And so we built up a huge workforce to pursue those opportunities. We still believe in those opportunities, but they're back on their original timeline. And actually, literally, if you look at a bunch of graphs that we have internally, it's literally the COVID boom and then, not bust really, but as it receded, everything's back on its original trajectory. (01:17:16): We didn't lose ground or lose time, but the pull forward didn't happen. Well, that means your economics don't make any sense anymore. Now, you made a bunch of investments that are going to yield too distant in the future, and getting there faster isn't going to help you and you're carrying a much extra cost. That sucks, man. It sucks. And we don't feel great about it. We really don't. It's a business, it's awful, and it happens. (01:17:41): I do think one thing that was interesting about that time was, for those of us who grew up and saw the .com boom firsthand, I was born and raised in the valley, so that was all around me when I was graduating high school and going to college, and then in the 2008 major recession on the housing crash and on the market and all that stuff. Now, let's imagine you graduated college in 2009-
turns.zh: 我们在业务运营方式上进行了重大调整，这过程极其痛苦。说到这，要追溯到新冠疫情后的繁荣时期，当时电商、远程工作和这些工具类产品（正如我们所开发的）等领域似乎迎来了一场持久的结构性变革，这为我们提供了机遇。我们为抓住这些机遇扩建了庞大的团队。我们至今仍坚信这些机遇，但它们已回归到原有的发展轨道上。实际上，从内部图表来看，这就像是新冠疫情引发的繁荣，随后在疫情消退后，一切又回归到原有的发展路径。（01:17:16）我们并未失去阵地或浪费时间，但向前推进的势头并未形成。这意味着我们的经济逻辑不再成立。现在，你做了很多投资，但回报要等很久才能兑现，更快实现目标也无济于事，还会背负额外成本。这太糟糕了，伙计。真的很糟糕。我们对此深感失望。这就是商业，残酷又无奈，但这种情况时有发生。（01:17:41）我确实认为那段时期有个有趣的现象。对于我们这些亲身经历过互联网泡沫的人来说，比如我在硅谷出生长大，那时正值高中毕业、上大学阶段。而2008年的房地产崩盘、市场危机等大事件又接踵而至。现在，让我们假设你2009年大学毕业——

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: ... all that stuff. Now let's imagine you graduated college in 2009 and got a job. Well shoot, you're 15 years in your career, you could be a director and you've never seen a downturn. I think we also had, in addition to what was very unfortunately conventional mis-forecasting in the business that caused us to over hire, that we had to correct for. You also had a workforce that was just not at all of a mentality that this could ever happen. This felt like it was an act of God when in fact it's like a cyclical nature of all businesses that this will happen at some time and you hope it doesn't and you wish it didn't, but you have to deal with it. And so I think we have a bit of a tough storm there for the whole industry and we're still feeling it. I think we're still feeling it. (01:18:45): Certainly we're happy at Meta to be beyond that point and we're growing again and executing at a stable rate and feeling really good about that, but quite a few of our other companies in the industry. And it's a very uncertain time for engineers, for PMs, for designers, for everyone and all the support functions around them. I'm super sympathetic for that. I think obviously the mis-forecasting that happened inside of Meta's walls happened everywhere and now that you have, especially with higher interest rates and cash isn't as cheap, runways are tighter. People are just making those pragmatic calls. I think we'll rally back from this. I think this is a normal thing that happens to industries, but it doesn't reduce my sympathy and empathy for those who have been affected by it or who live in fear of it.
turns.zh: 嗯，所有那些事。现在假设你2009年大学毕业后就找到了工作。天哪，你已经在职场打拼了15年，本可以成为总监了，却从未经历过低谷。我认为除了我们行业内普遍存在的错误预测（导致招聘过剩）需要纠正外，当时员工的心态也完全没有预料到这种情况会发生。当这场危机来临时，人们觉得像是天灾，但其实这是所有行业周期性规律，早晚会到来，尽管你希望它不会发生，但你必须面对它。所以我认为整个行业正经历着一场严峻的风暴，而且我们至今仍在承受其影响。我认为我们在Meta公司已经度过了最艰难的时期，现在又重新增长，运营稳定，感觉很不错，但行业内许多其他公司仍深陷困境。对工程师、产品经理、设计师以及所有支持部门来说，现在都是一个充满不确定性的时期。我对此深表同情。我认为Meta内部出现的错误预测在其他地方也普遍存在。现在利率上升，现金流更加紧张，发展空间受到限制，人们不得不做出务实的决策。我相信我们会从中恢复过来。这对行业来说是正常的周期，但这并不会减少我对受影响者或那些生活在恐惧中的人的同情和共鸣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was talking to a friend who works at Meta and I was asking them what it's like to work at Meta and she was just like, "It's intense, and it used to be more chill. There were people that were coasting here and there," and now she's like, "No, all those people are gone now. It's just only the intense people left and we're working really hard." Does that bring up anything?
turns.zh: 我和一位在Meta工作的朋友聊天，问她在Meta工作是什么感觉，她说"压力很大，之前没这么紧张。以前有些人在这里混日子"，但现在她说："不，那些人都走了。现在只剩下认真工作的人。"这让你有什么感触吗？

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Yeah. I don't want to comment on people who left. People left Meta for all kinds of different reasons and likewise role elimination happened in many cases because we just decided not to do this work at this point. We were going to do it two years from now and don't need to carry a team to do it. I think it's really hard to generalize because each of these is a specific person with a specific life and a story that is rich and deserves to be told. But I do think that if there was somebody coasting and you as a manager have to make tough calls on who you're bringing in which way you're going to bias my profound suspicion, and again, I don't know your friend who you spoke with, my profound suspicion is that person's probably already working hard. You know what I'm saying? That person's already probably working hard. I don't think we changed how hard any individual worked. I really don't believe that. (01:20:35): I do think there was a selection bias as to what was going to happen, and I think that's probably what you saw play. In fact, if there is a generality that can be found.
turns.zh: 是啊。我不想评论那些离职的人。人们离开Meta的原因各不相同，许多职位被裁掉也是因为我们决定现在不需要做某些工作了，而两年后才需要。我们原本计划两年后再做这些事，现在不需要维持团队了。我觉得很难一概而论，因为每个人都有独特的生活和故事，值得被讲述。但我确实认为，如果有人混日子，而你作为管理者不得不决定要引进谁，偏向谁，我会深表怀疑。再说，我不了解你提到的那个朋友，但我强烈怀疑那个人可能已经在努力工作了。你懂我的意思吧？那个人很可能已经在努力工作了。我不认为我们改变了任何个人的工作态度。我真的不这么认为。（01:20:35）：我确实认为对未来可能发生的事情存在选择性偏见，而这可能就是你所看到的。事实上，如果真能找到一个普遍规律的话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe as a last question, I have this segment where I call Failure Corner where I ask people to share a failure of their career and what they learned from that experience. Is there something that comes to mind?
turns.zh: 或许作为最后一个问题，我有个环节叫“失败角落”，邀请人们分享职业生涯中的失败经历以及从中获得的教训。你有没有什么想法？

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: I've failed tons of times. I've built products that nobody used. I've built technical architectures that didn't scale. I've failed all kinds of times. I don't regret most of those. Almost every one of those I learned from. It was a stop on the path to a better solution or it was a recognition that this thing wasn't going to work ever, which is its own kind of a gift. All the failures that I regret, that I take seriously are personal failures where I affected a person in a way that I'm not proud of, maybe wasn't proud of the time because I wasn't in control of my own emotions or mood. I was feeling fearful, I was feeling scared, and there's a bunch of these one or two that stand out that I don't feel comfortable sharing because the person affected, I think would prefer I didn't share. (01:21:46): I'll share one that was... I think the person's and I are tight now. We have this really silly discussion. I remember it so vividly. In the early days of client server architectures, which Facebook obviously is a website, so you're calling to a server to get the webpage, but then that server is going to call the other servers to gather things and that was one of the major clients of remote procedure calls because newsfeed ranking was all done on this other set of servers that had its own special requirements and special build and how it was put together. And so your main web server would put a call-out over a remote procedure, call to the remote server and get a response back. And we had this really janky RPC system that, I won't say who built it, but it was built and it was just a piece of garbage constantly failing. It was not robust at all. And one of our best engineers, Mark Sleek, built a new one called Thrift. It was a great, really great RPC infrastructure. (01:22:47): And one of my best friends, Dave Federman, one of my really good friends and a brilliant engineer, we were talking about how to do the encoding and I was like, "I want it to be binary encoding." I was like, "You should binary encoding. I want it to be super efficient on the wire," because I'm storing these RPCs. They do two jobs for us, one of which is the active RPC, but I also store the RPCs in a log and replay them to do the work that we were doing in newsfeed ranking. That's how it was done back in the day. It was all kind of asynchronous offline and so I wanted to be as tight as possible. My memory bandwidth was very limited and memory was so expensive back then and Dave Federman was like, "No, no, no, that's short-term thinking Boz, we should be using Linux style descriptors that are plain English language. Then you could look at the log, you can see what it is. It's possible memory bandwidth will get cheaper, but these logs being scrutable to development is going to be a better thing." This is nerd bait. (01:23:42): Those of you who have been engineers in this call, this is like Vim EMX. This is nerd bait. This goes deep. This is like a long old thing.
turns.zh: 我失败过无数次。我开发过没人用的产品，搭建过无法扩展的技术架构。我经历过各种各样的失败。但其中大部分我并不后悔，因为每一次失败都让我有所收获。它们要么是通往更优解决方案的垫脚石，要么让我意识到某个方案注定行不通——这本身也是一种收获。唯有那些让我追悔莫及、深感自责的失败，是我个人犯下的过错。这些失败源于我对他人造成的负面影响——比如情绪失控、心怀恐惧、行为失当等——其中有两三次至今仍令我难以启齿，因为受影响的人可能不愿我公开这些细节。（01:21:46）：我可以分享一个例子……如今我和那个人关系很好。我们常开玩笑提起这段往事。那是在客户端-服务器架构的早期阶段（Facebook显然是典型案例），用户访问网页时会调用服务器，但服务器又会调用其他服务器获取数据。这时远程过程调用（RPC）成为关键技术，因为新闻推送排序功能全由另一套服务器处理，这些服务器有特定的需求和架构。主服务器通过RPC向远程服务器发送请求并获取响应。当时我们开发的RPC系统糟糕透顶（我不会透露是谁开发的），性能不稳定，根本不稳定。我们最优秀的工程师马克·斯利克（Mark Sleek）开发了名为Thrift的全新RPC框架，堪称杰作。（01:22:47）：我的好友戴夫·费德曼（Dave Federman）也是位才华横溢的工程师。我们讨论编码方式时，我主张使用二进制编码：“应该用二进制编码，这样传输更高效。”因为我需要存储RPC日志。RPC既有实时请求，也用于离线排序。当时一切都是异步离线操作，所以我追求极致的内存占用效率。戴夫反驳道：“别想短期取巧，用Linux风格的描述符更合适。日志易读，内存占用也会降低。” 这真是技术宅的狂欢时刻。（01:23:42）：在座的工程师们，这就像Vim和Emacs之争，充满技术细节的深层探讨。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it. Keep it coming.
turns.zh: 我太爱这种讨论了。继续吧。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: It's a room full of engineers at the company and the company's not that big, and so there's probably half the engineers of the company in this room. I was yelling. Literally I'm turning red, I'm sweating. I'm so angry at Dave Federman for countermanding my proposal and I'm the major RPC customer. A couple things. This is so dumb. Mark Sleek just built two encoders. It's not that hard. You pick which encoder you want for your things. That's the easiest solution ever. Second thing is Dave was right, by the way. Within a year, the memory bandwidth definitely didn't matter relative to how inscrutable it was to try to get into these logs. I had to build a ton of extra custom software to parse the logs and understand what what's going on. But also it was a case where my identity was caught up in being right. And for those who don't know, identity threat is just the biggest... Your worst behavior is always going to come out when you think you're under identity threat. (01:24:51): When you feel like some core part of how you see yourself is in question, you will react with every ounce of your fiber to defend that conception of yourself because it's so expensive to reconceptualize who you are that you defend yourself. So my identity was being right. [inaudible 01:25:08] on the wrist. And it caused me to take one of my best friends, one of the best engineers I knew, a guy I literally lived with and getting a really embarrassing for me conflict, which everyone was just scratching their head like, "What is going on with Boz right now?" I looked like an unhinged crazy person. I remember the room, I remember where I was standing in the room. I remember everything about that moment and I had to go home and be like, "What the fuck was that? What happened?" I'm asking myself like, "What happened there?" And that was one of the many steps in the journey to recontextualizing what it was was not to be right and what meant to be open-minded and curious and how to engage in this competition. (01:25:47): I was 22. I don't make excuses for it now, but I remember there was a couple other examples like that in things that were less technical and more personal that I won't share, but I remember each of them vividly and those are the real failures for me.
turns.zh: 公司里满屋子都是工程师，而公司规模并不大，因此这间会议室里可能聚集了公司一半的工程师。我当时大喊大叫。说真的，我脸红耳赤，汗流浃背。我对戴夫·费德曼否决我的提案感到愤怒至极，而我可是 RPC 客户的重要代表。还有几件事。真是太蠢了。马克·斯利克刚刚搭建了两个编码器，这又有什么难的？你只需要根据需求选择合适的编码器，这简直是最简单的解决方案。另外，我得承认戴夫说得没错。一年之内，与解析日志的复杂性相比，内存带宽根本就不是问题。我不得不额外开发大量定制软件来解析日志并理解其中的信息。但更重要的是，我的自我认同感受到了威胁。可能有些听众不了解，身份威胁是职场中最致命的杀手。当你觉得自己的核心价值观受到质疑时，最糟糕的行为就会暴露无遗。（01:24:51）当你觉得自己的核心身份被质疑时，为了捍卫这种自我认知，你会拼尽全力反击，因为重塑自我认知的代价实在太高了。所以我当时执着于证明自己是对的。（01:25:08）我手腕上戴着手表。这导致我和一位挚友、一位我曾同住的顶尖工程师之间爆发了严重冲突，每个人都困惑不已，纷纷问：“博兹现在这是怎么了？” 我看起来就像个失去理智的疯子。我记得那个房间，记得自己当时的站位。我清晰地记得那一刻的一切，回家后我不得不反思：“这到底怎么回事？” 这就是我重新审视自我认知的旅程中众多挫折之一，明白对错并非最重要，保持开放好奇的态度、积极参与竞争才是关键。（01:25:47）那时我才 22 岁。虽然现在我不再为此找借口，但仍清楚记得还有其他类似的例子，虽然不涉及技术层面，而是更私人的事情，我就不一一分享了。但每段经历都历历在目，对我而言，这些才是真正的失败。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love how this story is so long ago at this point and it's still stuck with you and such an impact, I think.
turns.zh: 我很惊讶这个故事至今仍对你影响深远，而且影响力如此之大。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Oh, my god, I'll never forget that. It was embarrassing. And for those, that's the old quote, it's really one of the truest quotes, and I know it's cliche and sometimes cliches are cliches because they're good. It's like, "People, they don't remember what you said. They just remember how you made them feel." That's all anyone remembers is how you made them feel, and I think in that room, I made people feel unsafe, maybe. It was bad.
turns.zh: 天啊，我永远忘不了那一幕。太尴尬了。正如那句老话所说：“人们只记得你给他们留下的感觉。”在那个房间里，我可能让人们感受到了不安全感，这太糟糕了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like this concept of identity threat. They call this podcast episode identity threat.
turns.zh: 我喜欢身份威胁这个概念。他们把这期播客命名为《身份威胁》。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: There you go.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Boz, we started this episode with a billion questions. I have a billion and one questions now. I wish we could keep going, but I know we have to wrap this up. Is there anything you wanted to share or leave listeners with before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 博兹，我们这期节目一开始就提了无数个问题。我现在又有了无数加一个的问题。真希望能继续聊下去，但知道得结束了。在进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你有没有什么想和听众分享或留下的感悟？

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Well, in the off chance that we do end up labeling this episode, identity threat, let me give you what really was... I made a lot of breakthroughs with coaching, learning about the feeling inside of my own body when I was feeling that identity threat and learning techniques and tactics to reduce the likelihood I would feel it and how to deal with it when it happened and how to repair when I did, I went through all that stuff. I would say the greatest lesson I learned would come years later and it was just from observing somebody. Ami Vora who was a legendary, long time came in and worked on our development platform, then worked with me on ads for a long time and then was the PM lead for WhatsApp for a long time. She's since gone on to do even more great things outside the company. Working with her, it was like watching an alien because her and I were so different in our approach and she approached... (01:27:38): She could have the most profound disagreement with somebody in the world and they would say the thing that she thought was not just wrong, but crazy wrong and she would respond. She would say, "Fascinating. You have to tell me more about why you think that." And I can't do it justice, she meant it from the core of her being. She saw this schism between her and that person and it could have been personal, it could have been professional, it could have been anything. She saw this schism and how they saw the world and how she saw the world and rather than reacting as if it was a threat that somebody saw it differently or rather than reacting afraid that maybe she was wrong and had done things wrong before, she reacted with the most genuine and profound curiosity. I just watched it absolutely tear down walls between points of view. People felt immediately her genuine heartfelt curiosity and would lean in and that would cause them to be open-minded. (01:28:36): And if she was right, which by the way she usually was, then they would leave being like, "Oh, okay, I was wrong about that," but she also would change her mind and that was the key. Ever since then, I really have tried to model that. When I have a strong internal clinch, I try to embrace curiosity like, "Wow, we do not see this thing the same way. That is fascinating. Tell me why you see that." And that can be by personal feedback. Someone's like, "Hey boss, I don't think you talk enough." "Wow, you don't think I talk enough? That is unexpected. I would love to hear more about that because no one's ever said that to me," so I wanted to give that to anybody who might recognize this behavior in themselves. There's lots of things that you can do and you should do that work. (01:29:22): The work of improving yourself is always fruitful and satisfying and it pays off, as we discussed, in every aspect of your life with your family, with your friends, and professionally. This is one that I really thought was so great was just curiosity. Embracing curiosity in those moments of challenge has really completely changed my life and I owe that to Ami Vora.
turns.zh: 好吧，就算我们最终把这一集归类为"身份威胁"，我还是想跟你们分享我的真实经历……我通过教练指导获得了许多突破，学会了如何识别自己身体内部感受到的身份威胁，掌握了减少这种感觉的技巧和策略，以及应对其发生时的应对方法。我还学会了如何修复损伤。最重要的收获是多年后从观察他人中学到的。阿米·沃拉（Ami Vora）是一位传奇人物，她曾在我们的开发平台工作，与我合作广告项目多年，后来长期担任WhatsApp的项目经理。如今她已离开公司，去追寻更广阔的天地。与她共事就像观察外星人——我们的工作方法截然不同。她能与世界上最固执己见的人产生最激烈的分歧，即便对方的观点被她认为是错误甚至疯狂的，她仍会回应："太有意思了。你得跟我多讲讲你为什么这么想。" 她真心实意地说出这番话。她能识别出与对方的认知鸿沟，无论是个人恩怨还是工作分歧。她不会因为对方持不同意见而感到威胁，也不会因害怕自己可能犯错而退缩，而是以最真诚、最深切的好奇心去回应。我亲眼目睹她如何打破观点的隔阂。人们立刻感受到她真挚的求知欲，愿意敞开心扉。（01:28:36）如果她是对的——顺便说一句，她通常是对的——对方会离开时说"哦，原来我错了"，但她也会改变主意，这才是关键。从那以后，我一直努力效仿她的做法。当我内心深处有强烈的固执观念时，我会尝试保持好奇心，比如"哇，我们对这件事看法不同。这太有意思了。告诉我你为什么这么看。" 这可以来自个人反馈，比如有人说："嘿，老板，我觉得你说话不够多。""哇，你觉得我说话不够多？真意外。我很想听听你这么说是因为没人这么说过我。" 我想把这些分享给可能在自己身上发现这种行为的人。有很多你可以做而且应该做的事情都会奏效。（01:29:22）提升自己的工作总是富有成效、令人满足的，正如我们所讨论的，它会对你的生活方方面面产生积极影响——家庭、朋友和事业。这是我认为非常棒的一点，那就是好奇心。在挑战时刻拥抱好奇心，真的彻底改变了我的生活，这都要归功于阿米·沃拉。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, I love this example. It's basically an example of, "Yes, and?", but in a really... no one's going to be like, "Yes, and?" It's a really nice way of saying it, "Just fascinating. Tell me more."
turns.zh: 哇，我喜欢这个例子。基本上这就是"是的，然后呢？"的例子，但用一种非常……没人会说"是的，然后呢？"这是一种很好的表达方式，"太有意思了。多跟我讲讲。"

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Fascinating. You've got to tell me why, I want to understand it.
turns.zh: 太有意思了。你得告诉我为什么，我想了解它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Maybe that'll be the new title, fascinating.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个。也许这会成为新标题，太有意思了。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: There you go.
turns.zh: 好的，接下来是闪电问答环节。博兹，你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Anyway, with that, Boz, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 不管怎样，接下来是闪电问答环节，博兹。我们已经到了这个激动人心的环节。你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: I'm ready.
turns.zh: 我准备好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: First question, what are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 第一个问题，请你推荐两到三本你向他人推荐最多的书？

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: The Dream Machine, which is a tremendous history of pre-history, really of modern computing ostensibly following the life of J.C.R Licklider, but really it's much broader than that, is a tremendous missing piece of history in my opinion. I think in my discipline, in computer science, we were not properly educated. We learned about Alan Turing and we learned about some of the technical underpinnings of computer science theory, but the modern computer and the path to it is a profound and fascinating one, and it has particular resonance today as J.C.R Licklider's observation was human in the loop computing and I think we are now in human in the loop AI, and I think there's a tremendous resonance there. The second one is Good Inside, which is Dr. Becky's book, and again, I think it's a tremendous parenting book, but more than that, it does contain lessons for how we think about our own emotions and how we manage those, which I find to be useful in any context.
turns.zh: 《梦之机》，这是一本关于前史的宏大著作，实际上是现代计算史，表面上追随J.C.R.利克利德的人生轨迹，但实际上它的视野要广得多。在我看来，这本书填补了我们学科中一个重要的历史空白。在我的专业领域——计算机科学中，我们没有得到充分的教育。我们了解了阿兰·图灵，也学过一些计算机科学理论的基础知识，但现代计算机及其发展历程是一个深刻而迷人的课题。如今，J.C.R.利克利德关于“人机协作计算”的观点尤为贴切，而我们如今正处于“人机协作人工智能”的时代，这其中的共鸣令人惊叹。第二本是贝基博士的《内在美》，这本书不仅是一本出色的育儿书籍，更为我们如何看待自身情绪和管理情绪提供了深刻启示，无论在何种情境下都十分实用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing recommendations. She's also got an online community for people that-
turns.zh: 精彩的推荐。她还有一个线上社区，供那些——

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: She has a wonderful online community, she's very engaged in it. And for those parents out there, you're a little early for this Lenny, but you'll get there. Having little scripts that I'm reading on Instagram that when I'm in a moment of tremendous emotional challenge with my children, I have the words handy. They're just top of mind for me. They've been cashed in, right? They're primed, is a big game changer.
turns.zh: 她有一个很棒的线上社区，她在其中非常活跃。对于那些为人父母的人来说，虽然现在还早，但你们终将为人父母。那些我在Instagram上收藏的小段文字，当我与孩子们面对巨大情绪挑战时，总能派上用场。这些话语始终在我脑海中浮现。它们就像储备好的弹药，随时可以启用，真是改变游戏规则的存在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This will be for our parenting episode down the road.
turns.zh: 这将用于我们后续的育儿专题节目。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a favorite recent movie or TV show that you've really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 最近有没有你特别喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Yeah. This is super conventional, but Mandalorian. One of the things that's been fun about that is really my kids again is we watched it with my kids, so we had a chance to go on the Galactic Star Cruiser. Again, y'all know I am a genuine and true nerd through and through. Huge fan of Scott Trowbridge and his work at Star Wars service lands in Disney and also of that. And so before that we got our kids who were nine and six and watched all the movies together, and then we were watching Mandalorian together as a family, and it's super fun and it's fun to have that kind of lore, a connection. So it's not just the classic kids movies, but there's something more, and I think for them they feel like it's an adult kind of conversation they get to be a part of. I've really enjoyed that. And I think the world of Dave Filoni and John Favreau and the team that's building that universe out.
turns.zh: 有啊。这问题很老套，但我要说《曼达洛人》。这部剧的乐趣之一就是，我又能和孩子们一起看了。我们一起坐过银河星际巡洋舰。大家都知道，我是个彻头彻尾的书呆子。我是斯科特·特罗布里奇和他在迪士尼《星球大战》主题乐园工作的超级粉丝。之前，我们带着9岁和6岁的孩子一起看了所有《星球大战》电影，然后全家一起看《曼达洛人》。这真的很有趣，能和孩子们分享这些背景知识，建立这种联结。这些可不只是经典儿童电影，而是有更深层的意义。对他们来说，感觉自己参与了大人的谈话。我特别喜欢这种体验。我也非常欣赏戴夫·菲洛尼、约翰·法夫罗以及整个打造这个宇宙的团队。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is the way.
turns.zh: 就是这样。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: This is the way.
turns.zh: 就是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite interview question that you like to ask candidates that you're interviewing?
turns.zh: 你有没有最喜欢的面试问题，喜欢问面试的候选人？

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: One of the most important things that I always ask people is what people who've worked with them would say are their greatest strengths and weaknesses. I like this for a couple of reasons, not least of which is I often do follow up with references and I like to triangulate their awareness of how other people calibrate though. And also how they respond to criticism. Sometimes candidates surprise me. They say, "Hey, you'll hear this critique a lot from me. I don't think it's fair." That can be an okay answer, but they've got to be a pretty robust there. Or it's like, "Hey, this is something I'm working on, here's what I'm working on." But I also like to hear what they think their superpowers are. And too often a lot of attention in interviews is paid to weaknesses, which I care about because I want to know what the downside is. But way more important to me is like, "What are you awesome at? What is the thing that if I can just hitch a wagon and ride, that's what I want to know. Where's the superpower that you're crushing it at?" (01:33:22): And what's funny is people are pretty rarely give my reference checks. They're not that often accurate about what the critiques are, but they're usually pretty accurate about what their strengths are.
turns.zh: 我经常问求职者的一个重要问题是，与他们共事过的人会如何评价他们的最大优点和缺点。我这么做有几个原因，其中最重要的是，我通常会跟进他们的推荐信，同时想通过三角验证法来了解其他人对他们的评价。还有他们如何回应批评。有时求职者会让我感到惊讶。他们会说：“嘿，你会经常听到我提这种批评意见。我觉得这不公平。”这或许是个可以接受的回答，但他们得足够坦然。或者他们会说：“嘿，这方面我正在改进，下面是我正在努力的方向。”但我更想听他们认为自己的“超能力”是什么。在面试中，人们往往过多关注缺点——这固然重要，因为我想了解潜在风险。但对我来说，更重要的是：“你最擅长什么？如果我能借力你的优势，我会很感兴趣。你在哪方面表现得特别出色？”（01:33:22）有趣的是，人们很少提供可靠的推荐信。他们的缺点反馈通常不准确，但对自身优势的描述通常比较到位。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. I'm also a huge proponent of strengths and not worrying too much about your weaknesses.
turns.zh: 很有意思。我也非常推崇关注优势，而非过度纠结于缺点。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: But asking people to contextualize their performance through the team, that's so important. We do not achieve very much on our own.
turns.zh: 但让求职者从团队视角审视自己的表现，这一点至关重要。我们单打独斗很难取得显著成果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Communication is the job. Amazing. Is there a favorite product that you recently discovered that you love? And Meta products are acceptable answers.
turns.zh: 沟通本身就是工作。太棒了。你最近有没有发现特别喜欢的产品？推荐Meta的产品也可以。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: The Ray-Ban Meta glasses would be a tempting answer. The multimodal stuff, which I'm going to get in trouble because I've been teasing this for months on social media and it's still a closed beta, and it's like, "We're growing the beta slowly," but it's like, "People already really badly want it." It was probably one of the most magical things I've gotten to try recently. It's not totally fair because it's also not you can buy the Ray-Ban Meta glasses and very soon, I won't say when, but very soon they'll have this capability, but it's more fun to think outside of the box. All right, this is such a... I'm going to get in trouble for this answer because it's a bit of a pretentious one. I'm not a car guy, let me say that right now. I don't like cars. I don't care about cars. I want a car that works and doesn't break. All my cars growing up, had over a hundred thousand miles in them because we only ever had used cars. (01:34:38): They were constantly breaking down and the power steering would go out while you're driving and you have to [inaudible 01:34:43] the thing and the brakes would go out or you'd throw a rod. I've done it all. I just wanted a car. And so then I drove a Honda Accord that I bought for 10 years and then I drove a Tesla Model S for 10 years. And a Tesla model S had a thing happen to it while it was parked, I will get into that. I get a new car and again, I'm like, "I want to get an electric car." And I was like, "I'm going to get something nice. I'm going to get something nice. I want to get something nice." I'm driving a Mercedes-Benz AMG EQS, and I didn't know cars could be this nice. I grew up driving used cars and whatever, I did not know it was possible. It is the best augmented reality product I think you could buy in the market today. (01:35:29): With the heads of display, it puts your turn in three-dimensional space. It's got cameras facing your eyes, so it's positioned correctly on this display relative to your eyes, the turn. And so when you come up, it's like you're hitting a little wall, you got to turn before you hit the wall. And I was like, "Oh my God, I think this car has a great augmented reality." Not a car guy, and I'm not trying to flex on this car or whatever it is. I like it a lot. I didn't know they could be that nice, but the thing that I thought was so impressive was they did an amazing job with augmented reality in this car.
turns.zh: 雷朋Meta眼镜会是个很诱人的选择。这款多模态产品让我很头疼，因为我已经在社交媒体上调侃了好几个月，但它至今仍处于封闭测试阶段。他们一直说"我们在慢慢扩大测试规模"，但用户们显然已经迫不及待了。这是我最近体验过的最神奇的产品之一。不过不公平的是，目前还不能直接购买雷朋Meta眼镜。虽然很快（虽然我不能透露具体时间）但它们很快就会具备相关功能。不过跳出固有思维模式还是很有趣的。好吧，这个回答可能会让我惹上麻烦，因为它听起来有点自命不凡。我得承认，我对汽车不太感兴趣。说实话，我不喜欢车，也不在乎车。我只想要一辆性能稳定、不会出故障的车。我成长过程中开的二手车，大多跑了十几万英里（因为我们只买二手车）。那些车总是出各种毛病——比如开车时方向助力失灵、刹车失灵、连杆断裂……我都经历过。我只想要辆能正常开的车。后来我开了10年的本田雅阁，又开了10年的特斯拉Model S。但特斯拉停放时出了问题，具体细节我待会儿再说。现在我换了辆梅赛德斯-奔驰AMG EQS，我之前都不知道车能这么好。我开惯了二手车，对此完全没有概念。我认为这是目前市面上能买到的最棒的增强现实产品。（01:35:29）通过显示屏上的导航，它能把转弯路线投射到三维空间。摄像头对着你的眼睛，所以在显示屏上看到的转弯路线与你的视线是正确对应的。当你快要撞到障碍物时，系统会提示你转弯。我当时就感叹："天哪，这辆车增强现实功能太棒了。"虽然我对车不太在行，但我真心喜欢这款车。之前我从没想过车能做到这么好，但最让我惊叹的是，他们在车载增强现实技术上做得如此出色。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Mercedes-Benz, a player in the augmented reality, mixed reality space.
turns.zh: 哇。梅赛德斯-奔驰，在增强现实、混合现实领域的玩家。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Big time. They're out there, they're in the lead.
turns.zh: 非常厉害。他们走在前沿。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I sometimes think about having a contest where I give away products people mention in this segment, and now you've blown my budget way out of proportion.
turns.zh: 我有时会想搞个抽奖活动，送出这段节目中提到的产品，现在你已经让我的预算超支了。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Ray-Ban Metas, you can afford that.
turns.zh: 雷朋Meta眼镜，你买得起啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an amazing, I'm going to have to check that out. I think we're going to increase some sales for Mercedes. Next question. Do you have a favorite life motto that you often come back to think about, share with friends and family, find useful?
turns.zh: 太棒了，我得去看看。我觉得我们会为梅赛德斯带来不错的销量。下一个问题。你有没有一个经常回想、与朋友家人分享、觉得很有用的生活格言？

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Yeah. We have a funny actually how we came about this. The motto my family has, my immediate family, me, my wife and kids is just trust yourself. Just trust yourself. Actually, the reason we have that motto is when we have a house, we have a few nice art pieces and one of them is a Tracy Amen, a famous UK based artist, and she does neon pieces and it says, "Trust yourself." And so it's in our bedroom hallway where me and all the kids and my wife are, it says, trust yourself and every morning the neon lights up and it's trust yourself. And then I had the chance to have a crest made in the UK and my family's English from way back. And so in the crest it says, "Trust yourself." And I always talk to my kids, especially. I really think people, when you're experiencing peer pressure like, "Who do you trust? Them or yourself? When you're having a lot of self-doubt and uncertainty, you have to trust yourself." (01:37:17): I just think so much of the success I've had, I think this is probably true of most people who went to startups and succeeded, was like, "I just had faith that I was making good decisions." I mean, this comes back to the conviction point I made earlier about how you do things like newsfeed or controversial things or how you make big expensive changes, just conviction. You have to believe you, your eyes, ears in an intellect have combined to give you a point of view that has intrinsic value and deserves your respect as opposed to reading that newspaper article about your company and believing it over what your own eyes and ears have told you. That's the motto that we go with.
turns.zh:
是啊。我们怎么想到这个座右铭的，其实挺有趣的。我家人的座右铭——我、妻子和孩子们——就是“相信自己”。就是相信自己。实际上，我们之所以有这个座右铭，是因为我们家有几幅不错的艺术品，其中一幅是英国知名艺术家特雷西·阿门（Tracy Amen）的作品，她擅长创作霓虹灯艺术品，上面写着“相信自己”。这幅作品挂在我们卧室走廊里，里面有我、孩子们和妻子，每天早晨霓虹灯亮起时，都会闪现“相信自己”的字样。

后来我有机会在英国定制了家族纹章，追溯我们家族的英国血统。纹章上也写着“相信自己”。我尤其会跟孩子们强调这一点。我真的觉得，当人们面临同辈压力时，比如“你信任谁？他们还是你自己？”当你充满自我怀疑和不确定性时，就必须相信自己。

（01:37:17）：我认为我取得的很多成功——我想对大多数成功的创业者来说都是如此——都源于一句简单的话：“我只是坚信自己做出了正确的决策。” 这又回到了我之前提到的信念点——无论是处理新闻推送、处理有争议的事情，还是进行重大昂贵的变革，都需要信念。你必须相信自己，相信你的眼睛、耳朵和智慧所形成的观点，认为它具有内在价值，值得尊重，而不是盲目听信报纸上关于自己公司的报道。这就是我们的座右铭。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I think it's also important to say you won't always be right and that's okay.
turns.zh: 我还想说，人不可能永远正确，但这没关系。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Totally. That's right. Trusting yourself also includes taking risks because you trust that you can deal and handle with what happens when the risks don't pay out.
turns.zh: 完全正确。相信自己也包括敢于冒险，因为你相信自己能应对风险带来的后果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Beautiful. Final question. I know that you're an amateur photographer, maybe semi-pro photographer, a lot of travel photography.
turns.zh: 太棒了。最后一个问题。我知道你是个业余摄影师，或许是半职业摄影师，拍了很多旅行照片。

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Amateur. Amateur, amateur.
turns.zh: 业余的。业余，业余。

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.speaker: Andrew ‘Boz’ Bosworth
turns.en: Art is actually a great place to talk about trusting yourself, by the way. And I know it's cheesy to say it, but I think Rick Rubin's recent interviews on what art is and how people make it is spot on. You have to make it for yourself and you have to love it. And if someone else loves it and it finds broader resonance, that's awesome, but that's not why you do it. And if you start to try to do it for broader resonance, then you're kind of chasing something else. It's media, it's entertainment, but it's not art. It's some other thing. And I say all this to basically tap dance and say, I kind of love a lot of my photos and it's very hard to pick a favorite. The one that is popping to my head, which has more emotional [inaudible 01:39:12] is a picture I took of my son playing in the street and just jumping in a puddle, wearing a rain boot, rain slick kind of a thing. And it's not sharp, it's not in focus. It's a vignette, it's an idea. (01:39:27): And I really do think Ansel Adams talked a lot about how the goal of the photographer is to create a capture that expresses to the viewer what it felt like to be there. And people forget that he was a master of the dark room even more so than maybe than the capture, the print. The print was where he did amazing work. And I've had the pleasure to go to his dark room in Big Sur and spend time with his son and watch them do development in that room. And he had elaborate scripts of how he would highlight, dodge and burn different parts of the photograph to get it to have the resonance that he wanted. And he fought for photography to be accepted as an artistic medium, which it wasn't, which I find so resonant in today's AI art conversations where once again, we're trying to gate keep what is art and you just don't get to do that unfortunately. (01:40:20): So this picture of my son, no one would call it a technical marvel, but as a vignette of it capturing for me personally, but also I think in general for parents, the ephemerality of these tremendously touching, charming human moments that you have with your children, that's the one that comes to mind.
turns.zh:
顺便说一句，艺术其实是个谈论如何相信自我的绝佳场所。虽然这么说有点老生常谈，但我觉得里克·鲁宾（Rick Rubin）最近关于艺术是什么以及人们如何创作艺术的访谈真是说到了点子上。你必须为自己而创作，也必须热爱自己的作品。如果别人喜欢你的作品，并且它能引发更广泛的共鸣，那当然很棒，但这不该是你创作的初衷。如果你开始为了迎合大众口味而创作，那就偏离了正轨。这是媒体，是娱乐，但不是艺术。  

说这些主要是想强调，我确实很喜欢自己的很多照片，但要选出一张最爱实在太难了。现在浮现在我脑海里的一张照片，充满了情感（1:39:12），是我拍的儿子在街上玩耍的场景——他穿着雨靴，在雨水坑里跳来跳去。这张照片并不清晰，焦点也不准，但它是一个意境，一个构想。（1:39:27）我深信安塞尔·亚当斯（Ansel Adams）曾多次强调，摄影师的目标是向观者传达身临其境的感觉。人们往往忽略了，他对暗房技术的掌握甚至比拍摄和冲印更为精湛。冲印环节才是他真正展现才华的地方。我曾有幸参观他在Big Sur的暗房，看着他和儿子一起冲洗照片。他会用复杂的技巧来提亮、遮光和过度曝光不同区域，以达到理想的艺术效果。他曾为摄影争取被视为艺术媒介的认可，而当时人们对此并不认同，这让我联想到当下关于AI艺术的争论——我们又在试图给艺术设限，可惜这种做法注定失败。  

至于我儿子的这张照片，没人会说它是技术杰作，但作为个人记录，也是我认为所有父母都会感同身受的——与孩子共度这些稍纵即逝却又无比珍贵的温馨瞬间。这张照片正是这种情感的写照。
